  2. A 1 to 3-person dev studio, an open-source project, or a small AI SaaS startup cannot afford age-verification integration, specialized liability insurance, and endless legal audits. They are instantly outlawed in the European single market.
  3. Crown kings of digital feudalism: The draft turns App Stores into legally required age-verifiers and application censors. Apple and Google become the guardians of user identity and app filtering, which gives them feudal power over the software peasants.

This show the spirit of the . Instead of tearing down 's walled garden, Brussels helps them build a fortress with moats.

The shadow landlords: who really collects the rent on the moat

Following the money pipe’s beginning, and the picture gets uglier.

Who owns , , , and ? Look at the investors and the same names keep surfacing among the largest holders: , , . alone manages more than $15 trillion.

These are not venturers hunting for the next disruptor. They are just mid-age landlords. Invest money buys the entire market and collects rent as long as the biggest tenants stay on top. A scrappy startup that could crack 's walled garden is not "innovation" on that balance sheet. It is a risk to the profit. And a regulation that cold-blooded kills a thousand such startups before they ship? That is free insurance. Ultimately, they built a mechanism for infinite enrichment.

I can't show you a memo with 's logo on the . Nobody has to be bribed when every incentive points the same way.

Here is how the system actually runs. Brussels "consults stakeholders." The stakeholders who show up are the ones with permanent offices, accredited lobbyists, and €* million budgets. Fact: According to a June 2026 study by and Corporate Europe Observatory, big tech now tops the lobbying league table in Brussels at roughly . The indie dev with a day job and an old build server is not on the invite list. The 's own “transparency” register is voluntary and has no effective sanctions, so nobody can even verify what is really being spent. Call it corruption with legalized bribery: polite and invisible.

Everyone at the table wins:

  • gets levers of control: identity checks, age verification, and reporting pipelines.
  • get a legally mandated moat, and the title of chief warden on top.
  • The shareholders behind them get decades of predictable cash flow with competition regulated out of existence.
  • get a choice: die, or kneel before the platforms.

Call it a conspiracy and they will laugh you out of the room - and they'd be right, because it isn't one. It is worse: it is the system working exactly as designed. So show me the stakeholder meeting list for the Kids Act. Show me who was in the room. Until then, ask the only question that matters: who benefits?

The verdict: stop enforcing monopolists, start enforcing the law

The 's tech policy is fundamentally hypocritical:

  • "We stand with startups and open-source against monopolies!"
  • Years of stalling on direct evidence of hardware-tying, paired with a wave of legislation that makes running an independent tech business in Europe almost impossible.

By tying software distribution to multi-million-dollar infrastructure, the EU isn't curbing monopolies - it is outlawing competition. It’s digging a deep moat around , , and , ensuring no challenger can ever threaten them, or the shareholders who collect the rent.

If the Commission wants the developer community to take the seriously, it must stop print regulation nightmares for indie devs and start enforcing the law against who admit in writing that build pipeline doesn't need their hardware.

Thanks for reading. Hang in there, guys

items.title: The Hidden Work Behind Building an App With AI Coding Agents
items.author: Paul Gendek
items.content:
I returned to a browser music project in September 2026 after its initial feature work had spent months in the background. AI agents made it possible to coordinate implementation, checks and browser validation in parallel. That changed the work I needed to do: keep the product direction clear, make physical-device findings part of the requirements and organize a review queue I could manage.

I am the creator of Mock Band and have a vested interest in the project. AI tools drafted this article from my original interview and the current case study. Agents implemented product changes and ran automated checks; I owned product direction, requirements, physical-device acceptance testing and merge approval.

A practical reason to begin

The project began with a small interruption in something I enjoyed. When I was jamming alone on guitar, changing a metronome or backing groove meant stopping, reaching for the laptop and then trying to recover the idea. With bandmates, I could call for a new key or signal a change while keeping my hands on the instrument.

In a note dated September 17, 2023, I described choosing drums, bass and guitar accompaniment, repeating a groove and reshaping it through follow-up instructions. A footswitch would activate voice listening. I named the project Mock Band and sketched logo ideas on graph paper.

The player would supply the riff and direction. The software would supply an adjustable rhythm section. I wanted deliberate control of accompaniment, not a system that listened to a guitar and automatically followed its performance.

That was a product idea before it was an implementation. The earliest preserved repository commit is from August 2025, although local work may have preceded it. The first product effort took place during parental leave. Repository history supports early Cursor use and later Copilot involvement.

My recollection of that period is prompting the implementation rather than manually writing source code. The contribution I can clearly claim is the concept, platform choice, brand, requirements and acceptance testing. Naming those responsibilities precisely makes the development story easier to assess.

One of the most useful findings came from a purchased Bluetooth footswitch. The interaction had assumed hold-to-talk. The physical device behaved as a toggle.

I could not solve that mismatch by asking whether the code looked plausible. I had to try the switch, describe what it did and feed the result back into Cursor. The interaction was refined around a tap that starts listening while recognition is awaited. It took debugging and repeated manual testing to get it usable.

Recalling scenes with the footswitch was a particularly satisfying early result for me. That is an account of using an earlier build, not a promise about every controller or the current release.

The experience clarified a responsibility I still had even when implementation was assisted. A requirement about a physical gesture has to survive contact with the physical object. The software can consistently implement an assumption that the device immediately disproves.

Returning changed the way I could organize work

Life pushed the project into the background after the initial feature work. There was later maintenance, including a security update. I returned in September 2026 as musical and creative activity picked up toward fall.

With Codex, I could coordinate background tasks across implementation, automated checks, browser validation and operational setup. I no longer had to wait for one closely supervised thread before another task could begin.

That gave me a different workflow, but it also created review pressure. More work could arrive for my attention, and some fixes caused regressions. The existence of an agent-produced change did not settle whether I wanted it in the product.

I required QA steps in pull request descriptions and retained human merge approval. GitHub's review documentation describes the practical distinction between commenting, approving and requesting changes. In my workflow, the merge decision remained a separate responsibility from producing the proposed implementation.

When the queue became overwhelming, I asked for related pull requests and manual checks to be combined into batches. The improvement was a review process I could manage. I did not measure a productivity multiplier, so I would not turn that experience into a claim about how many times faster a model made me.

A feature can be implemented before it is accepted

The current product uses React and TypeScript for its interface and state. Text and recognized speech share a command vocabulary, while mapped MIDI actions connect to state and scene handlers. An audio bridge passes changes to an AudioWorklet, which renders drums, bass and rhythm accompaniment and handles timing.

AudioWorklet's separate audio execution context helps explain why interface rendering and musical timing have distinct responsibilities. Knowing that an architecture contains those components is still different from accepting how it feels during practice.

Musical changes can queue for beat or bar boundaries. Scenes and preferences stay in the browser, with JSON backup and import. These choices create real review questions: does the interface make a pending change understandable, and does a player know where a saved configuration will be available?

Some of those questions can be checked through software behavior or a browser inspection. Some require listening. A physical-controller question requires the relevant hardware. A question about useful practice needs someone to practice.

Agents handled automated unit tests and other validation. I supplied manual acceptance testing and merge decisions. That does not mean I manually tested every pull request, or that the maintained release gate certified every legacy test and device combination.

I also reported a successful live MIDI output test through an IAC bus into Logic Pro on September 29, 2026. It supports that particular route. It is not proof that every physical MIDI receiver works.

The most useful review question became specific: what does this check establish, and what remains outside it? Without that boundary, an implementation result can silently become a broader product claim.

Product judgment also changed access

The original early-access gate asked people for an email before they could use the app. The list was not growing, and I felt that collecting addresses offered little value while potentially discouraging use. During the September refresh, I chose immediate access. Updates became an optional, confirmed signup.

That was a product decision. Agents could implement it, but they did not establish whether it was the right tradeoff. I needed to decide what mattered at this stage and accept what I was giving up.

It also changed what I wanted to learn. Opening an app is different from starting audio, and starting audio is different from a useful musical session. Even uninterrupted playback does not demonstrate that someone played guitar or found recurring practice value.

Product and distribution were changing together, so I cannot claim that removing the gate caused growth or improved retention. The early playback evidence is observational.

Keep the public story within the evidence

The same discipline matters when describing the work. HackerNoon's second-human rule treats another person's review as a step before ordinary publication. That offers a useful parallel to the review boundary in my project, without making editorial review and software acceptance identical.

In either setting, production and acceptance are different events. An article can sound convincing without its claims being established. A change can pass an automated check without its musical behavior being acceptable. Another review step is valuable only if the reviewer knows which judgment it is supposed to supply.

For the current version, I have not yet established a regular practice routine beyond QA. An original-riff jam-session reel and voluntary practice trials are next steps, not completed outcomes. I cannot claim learning gains, sustained use by guitarists or a broader hardware pass.

The project referenced here is Mock Band, an adjustable browser backing band. It is free to use without an account, with voice and MIDI capabilities subject to browser and device limits. That describes its current access model, not evidence that it has solved the practice problem for other musicians.

Returning to the project gave me more implementation capacity and a clearer view of the work that stayed with me. I had to choose the requirements, confront physical-device behavior, keep review manageable and decide what was ready to merge. The next milestone is evidence of recurring musical value. I want the review process to leave enough room to learn that.

Disclosure: I created Mock Band and have a vested interest in it. This is an AI-drafted account based on my original interview and the current case study. I directed the product and retained merge approval; agents implemented changes and ran automated checks.

items.title: Essentials of Path Planning for Autonomous Vehicle Systems
items.author: vishwa vimukthi gammuduwaththage
items.content:
I build navigation software for drones that can't rely on GPS. Whenever I explain that work, I end up explaining the same thing first: where path planning sits in an autonomous system, and why it's harder than "find the shortest route." This is that explanation, written once, properly.

The examples lean on self-driving cars because that's where the literature is deepest. Everything here carries over to drones, ground robots, and boats, with a few differences I'll cover near the end.

Why autonomy, and why now

Autonomous driving is an old idea. Experiments with radio-controlled "driverless" cars date back to the 1920s. What changed in the last decade is that sensors became cheap, compute moved to the edge, and deep learning made perception actually work.

The safety argument is the one you hear most. You'll often see the claim that around 94% of crashes are caused by human error. That number comes from NHTSA, and NHTSA itself warns that it describes the last failure in the chain before a crash, not blame. The direction is still right: most crashes involve a human misjudgement somewhere, and a machine that never gets tired or distracted has room to do better. "Room to do better" is the honest version.

The stack in sixty seconds

Most autonomous driving systems are described as six layers:

  1. : cameras, LiDAR, radar, IMU, GNSS collect raw data.
  2. : turns raw data into objects, lanes, and free space.
  3. : works out where the vehicle is in the world.
  4. : estimates danger and predicts what other road users will do.
  5. Path planning & decision-making: chooses where to go and how.
  6. : turns the plan into steering, throttle, and braking.

The planner sits at layer five, which means it inherits every mistake made above it. A good planner is therefore as much about handling uncertain inputs as it is about clever search. So before getting to planning, here's what it's being fed.

What the planner sees: sensors

Colour, texture, semantics; cheap

No direct depth; struggles at night and in harsh shadows

Depth from two cameras a known baseline apart

Fails on low-texture surfaces; accuracy drops with distance

Structured light / ToF camera

Depth via projected IR pattern or light round-trip time

Short range; sunlight interference outdoors

Per-pixel brightness changes, asynchronously; microsecond latency, ~120 dB dynamic range

Unusual data format; tooling still maturing

360° view from fisheye arrays

Needs careful multi-camera calibration

Range and relative velocity, robust in rain and fog

Dense 3D point clouds from laser pulses

Cost; degraded by heavy rain, fog, dust

Radar and LiDAR share a basic idea: emit a signal and measure what comes back. FMCW radar sweeps the frequency of radio waves and computes range from the frequency difference between the transmitted and returned signal. LiDAR uses infrared laser light, either scanned mechanically or, increasingly, with solid-state and flash designs that have no spinning parts.

No sensor is good at everything, which is why production vehicles fuse several. That fusion is also the first place uncertainty enters the planner's world.

What the planner sees: perception

Perception converts sensor data into things a planner can reason about:

  • finds cars, pedestrians, signs, and lights in images and draws bounding boxes around them, usually with CNN- or transformer-based detectors.
  • comes in two flavours. segmentation labels every pixel with a class ("road", "car"). segmentation goes further and separates individual objects, giving each car its own pixel mask.
  • adds depth from stereo, LiDAR, or radar. Grouping sparse 3D points into clean objects is still hard.
  • follows moving objects over time to estimate their velocity and heading. This is what lets the system predict where things will be, not just where they are. Fusing multiple sensors here, often into an occupancy grid, is standard.
  • is its own problem because lanes are continuous surfaces, not objects. The usual pipeline is: preprocess the raw data, extract lane features, fit continuous curves (splines and similar models), then smooth the result over time using the vehicle's motion.

What the planner sees: localisation

The planner needs to know where the vehicle is to within centimetres. Three approaches dominate:

  • The IMU (gyroscope, accelerometer, magnetometer) tracks motion but drifts over time. GNSS corrects the drift but is only accurate to a few metres without augmentation, and it vanishes in tunnels and urban canyons. Good as an initial estimate, not enough on its own.
  • SLAM (Simultaneous Localisation and Mapping) builds a map and localises within it at the same time. uses cameras and is cheap and rich in landmarks but sensitive to lighting and texture. produces accurate point-cloud maps at higher cost. I've written separately about building a VSLAM pipeline
  • matches live sensor data against a pre-built high-definition map, either by point-cloud matching or by recognising known landmarks such as signs and road markings.

This layer is personal for me. My company builds a vision-only navigation SDK for drones in GPS-denied environments, and the core lesson from that work is simple: a planner is only as good as the pose estimate it's given. If localisation is off by a metre, a "collision-free" path isn't.

What the planner sees: risk and intent

The assessment layer asks two questions: how dangerous is the current scene, and what are the other agents about to do?

That covers detecting unsafe lane changes, predicting cut-ins, and classifying driving styles (an aggressive driver behind you behaves differently from a cautious one). Older systems used clustering methods such as PCA and k-means, or SVMs and small neural networks. Modern stacks increasingly use learned trajectory-prediction models that output several possible futures for each agent, with probabilities.

Those multiple futures are the planner's most important input, and its biggest headache.

Here's the core of the article. "Path planning" is really three nested problems running at different speeds.

1. Global (route) planning

Which roads take me from A to B? This runs on a road graph built from an offline map, recalculates rarely, and is basically solved. Dijkstra's algorithm and A* handle it, with tricks such as contraction hierarchies making continent-scale routing fast.

One correction to a claim I made in the original version of this article: finding the shortest path on a graph is not NP-hard. Dijkstra solves it in polynomial time. What's genuinely hard is in continuous space, which has been known since the late 1970s to be PSPACE-hard. That's where the difficulty lives, in the next two layers.

Given the route and the scene, what should the vehicle ? Keep the lane, change lanes, yield, overtake, stop, creep forward at an occluded junction. This used to be done with finite state machines and rule trees. It's increasingly learned or handled by search over candidate manoeuvres, because rules explode in number once you hit real traffic.

3. Local (motion) planning

Given the chosen behaviour, what exact trajectory should the vehicle follow for the next few seconds? It must be:

  • , against obstacles that move and react;
  • , meaning a car can't turn on the spot, and curvature and acceleration have limits;
  • , with low jerk and no wobbling;
  • , typically replanned every 50–100 ms.

This is where most of the engineering effort goes.

Graph search on a discretised world. Chop the space into a grid or lattice and search it. A* is the workhorse: it explores nodes in order of cost so far + estimated cost to go, and with an admissible heuristic it's guaranteed to find the optimal path. Here's a minimal version on a 4-connected grid:

import heapq

def astar(grid, start, goal):
    """4-connected grid A*. grid[r][c] == 1 means blocked."""
    def h(p):  # Manhattan distance: admissible on a 4-connected grid
        return abs(p[0] - goal[0]) + abs(p[1] - goal[1])

    open_heap = [(h(start), 0, start)]
    came_from = {start: None}
    g = {start: 0}

    while open_heap:
        _, cost, node = heapq.heappop(open_heap)
        if node == goal:
            path = []
            while node is not None:
                path.append(node)
                node = came_from[node]
            return path[::-1]
        if cost > g[node]:
            continue  # stale heap entry
        r, c = node
        for nr, nc in ((r + 1, c), (r - 1, c), (r, c + 1), (r, c - 1)):
            if 0 <= nr < len(grid) and 0 <= nc < len(grid[0]) and grid[nr][nc] == 0:
                new_cost = cost + 1
                if new_cost < g.get((nr, nc), float("inf")):
                    g[(nr, nc)] = new_cost
                    came_from[(nr, nc)] = node
                    heapq.heappush(open_heap, (new_cost + h((nr, nc)), new_cost, (nr, nc)))
    return None

Grid A* ignores vehicle dynamics, so cars use , which searches over continuous position and heading using motion primitives a real vehicle can drive. It was made famous by Stanford's entry in the 2007 DARPA Urban Challenge and is still common in parking and low-speed manoeuvring.

Instead of discretising everything, randomly sample the space and connect feasible samples. grows a tree quickly toward unexplored space; adds rewiring so the path converges toward optimal as samples increase; builds a reusable roadmap. These shine in high-dimensional or cluttered spaces, which is why they're popular for drones and robot arms. The trade-off is jittery paths that need smoothing.

Lattice and Frenét-frame planners. On structured roads, express motion relative to the lane centreline (along-road distance and lateral offset), generate a fan of candidate trajectories, score each one for safety, comfort, and progress, and pick the best. Simple, fast, interpretable, and widely used in highway driving.

Optimisation-based planning. Treat the trajectory as an optimisation problem: minimise a cost (deviation, jerk, time) subject to constraints (dynamics, collision avoidance). Model Predictive Control (MPC) solves this repeatedly over a short receding horizon, so it naturally blurs the line between planning and control. The catch is that collision constraints are non-convex, so solvers need good initial guesses, often supplied by one of the methods above.

Train a network to output trajectories directly, usually by imitating expert driving and increasingly refined with reinforcement learning. Since 2024, the most active line of research has been , which generate trajectories through iterative denoising. They're appealing because driving is multimodal: at a junction, "go left" and "go right" are both valid, and regression-based models tend to average the two into "go straight into the wall." DiffusionDrive (CVPR 2025) and Diffusion Planner (ICLR 2025) are good entry points.

In practice, production systems mix these: search or sampling for a coarse answer, optimisation to make it smooth and feasible, and learned components to predict others and score options.

The 2025–26 shift: end-to-end

The biggest change since I first wrote about this topic in mid-2025 is how far the industry moved toward systems, where perception, prediction, and planning are trained together, from sensor input to trajectory output.

Tesla replaced most of its hand-written planning code with neural networks in FSD v12. Waymo published EMMA in 2024, a research model built on Gemini that maps camera input directly to planner trajectories. Then in late 2025 Waymo described its production driver as a foundation model trained end-to-end. Waymo's framing is the useful one: end-to-end is a training strategy, not an architecture. You can keep distinct modules and still propagate gradients through all of them.

So the six-layer diagram above isn't wrong. It just describes the in the system, not necessarily separate pieces of code anymore.

Drones and other vehicles: what changes

Most of my own work is in the air, so a few differences worth knowing:

  • , and often unstructured, with no lanes and no road graph. Sampling planners (RRT*) and polynomial trajectory optimisation (minimum-snap) are more common than lattice planners.
  • Dynamics are fast and unforgiving. A quadrotor can't stop instantly, and a planning delay of 100 ms at speed is a real distance.
  • Compute and weight budgets are tight. You can't carry a car's GPU rack on a 250 g drone, so efficiency matters more than benchmark scores.
  • GNSS jamming and spoofing are now a routine problem in contested airspace. That's exactly why we build vision-only navigation at FromSky.

When I reverse-engineered a cheap RC drone to make it autonomous <!-- LINK: RC drone reverse-engineering article -->, the planner was the easy part to write and the hard part to trust. Every planning failure I hit traced back to state estimation, not the search algorithm.

The case against everything I just said

It would be easy to end with "end-to-end won, learn everything." The evidence is more mixed than that.

The steelman for modular, rule-based planning: In the 2023 nuPlan planning challenge, a team showed that a simple rule-based planner (PDM-Closed, essentially lane-following with a carefully tuned speed and safety model) matched or beat much more complex learned planners in closed-loop evaluation. Separately, researchers showed that common open-loop benchmarks on nuScenes could be "solved" surprisingly well using little more than the vehicle's own past motion. Learned planners often look better on paper than on the road. Modular systems also have something end-to-end systems struggle with: you can inspect each stage, test it in isolation, and prove certain safety properties. Regulators and safety engineers care about that.

The steelman for end-to-end: Hand-written rules don't scale to the long tail. Every edge case adds rules, and the rules start conflicting. A learned system improves with data, and the companies with the most driving data have bet heavily on it. Diffusion planners and RL fine-tuning are also directly attacking the weaknesses that rule-based baselines exposed.

hybrid. Use learning where the world is too complex to write down, such as prediction, scoring, and generating candidate trajectories. Keep a verifiable layer underneath that can veto unsafe plans: collision checks, kinematic limits, hard safety rules. For safety-critical vehicles, and especially for anything airborne, I want a planner that can explain why it crash.

Path planning is the moment an autonomous system commits to an action. Everything upstream, including sensors, perception, localisation, and prediction, exists to make that commitment a good one. The algorithms are well understood. The open problems are about uncertainty, interaction with other agents, and trust.

If you're starting out, implement A* on a grid, then Hybrid A*, then RRT* in a simulator. You'll learn more about why planning is hard from watching your own planner fail than from any survey, including this one.

items.title: Designing a Claims Intake Platform
items.author: sai
items.content:
"Design the claims experience" is a deceptively broad prompt. A carrier's claims platform spans intake, fraud detection, estimating, payments, subrogation, and correspondence — hours of material. In a 45-minute interview, the real skill isn't covering everything; it's scoping hard, picking the two flows that matter, and designing them end to end. I chose filing a claim (first notice of loss, or FNOL) and the adjuster work queue.

I start by writing the requirements down so the interviewer and I agree on scope. Functionally: let a policyholder file a claim and upload damage photos and documents; process those into derived artifacts (thumbnails for fast review, an input for an ML damage-estimate model, OCR'd text from documents, a virus scan); score and prioritize open claims into each adjuster's work queue; and support mobile and web. Non-functionally: high availability, durability (never lose a claim or a photo), an auditable trail for compliance, eventual consistency, horizontal scalability, and low latency for adjuster productivity. Durability and auditability quietly drive most of the design.

— The two flows: claim intake / write path (top) and the precomputed adjuster work queue / read path (bottom).

Flow 1 — Filing a claim (FNOL)

The key decision is to keep large media off my own servers. When a policyholder files, the app calls a claims-intake microservice through a load balancer. The service does two cheap things: it writes a claim metadata row (claimID, policyID, lossDate, docLink, status, timestamp) to a SQL store, and it returns a pre-signed S3 URL with a short expiry. The client then uploads the damage photos and documents directly to S3 — my services never handle the bytes. I deliberately avoid putting the media into a message queue; a batch of high-resolution photos would blow up queue memory.

Raw uploads aren't useful until they're processed. I trigger this with change data capture: the insert into the metadata table fires a CDC event that fans work out to a pool of processing workers. Each worker pulls the media from S3 and produces the derived artifacts — thumbnails, an ML damage-estimate input, OCR text, a virus scan — writing the results back to S3 and recording the new links in the table. The intake tier itself is sharded by a hash key (~100 shards) and fronted by load balancers, so it scales horizontally and stays stateless.

Ranking every adjuster's worklist on each dashboard load is too slow, so I precompute. A Scoring Service ranks open claims by severity, SLA urgency, complexity, and fraud signal, and an async job runs near-real-time to produce, per adjuster and skill queue, a Top-K prioritized list. The Queue Generation Service stores these lists in a NoSQL key-value store, keyed by (adjuster, queue).

When an adjuster opens the dashboard, we don't rank anything live: we return their precomputed worklist through the load balancer. Reads stay fast, the queue stays current enough under eventual consistency, and the expensive scoring happens off the request path — for example, adjuster "sai" opens the auto physical-damage queue and immediately sees the highest-priority open claims.

What an interviewer wants to hear

My first pass leaves room to sharpen a few decisions, and these are the ones that land:

In system design, scoping is the skill. Two flows designed cleanly — direct-to-S3 uploads, CDC-triggered processing, and a precomputed work queue — beat ten boxes drawn without depth. That focus is what carries an interview, and it is exactly how you'd build the real platform.

1. Amazon S3 User Guide, "Sharing objects with presigned URLs" — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html

2. Debezium documentation (change data capture) — https://debezium.io/documentation/

3. Martin Fowler, "Audit Log," Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture — https://martinfowler.com/eaaDev/AuditLog.html

AI Disclosure: AI tools were used for research assistance, reference gathering, and editorial support. The author reviewed, verified, and approved the final content.

items.title: What Did Your AI Agent Actually Do? Building a Tamper-Evident Audit Trail
items.author: Vikas Luthra
items.content:
SHA-256 hash chains, Merkle trees, boundary capture, and the engineering behind AgentLedger

An AI agent just priced a deal, approved a transaction, or updated a customer record. Months later, someone asks a simple question: what did the agent actually do, and can you show that the record has not been changed since?

That second question is easy to underestimate. Traditional automation is usually governed by predefined logic that can be inspected and tested. Agent decisions can depend on probabilistic model output and the state the agent saw at that moment. Re-running the same request later may produce a different path. That makes the contemporaneous record unusually important.

I built AgentLedger to make changes to that recorded history detectable. This article is about the engineering behind it: structured action records, deterministic serialization, SHA-256 hash chains, Merkle sealing, verification, where capture happens, and the limits of what the design can prove.

One framing note before the code. This does not replace observability tools like OpenTelemetry. Those tell an operator how the system ran and help you debug it. AgentLedger answers a different question: giving the organization a checkable record of what was captured about the autonomous actor’s actions. With an independent external anchor, that record can also be verified against a reference outside the system that stores it.

Disclosure: I am the author of AgentLedger, the open-source project described in this article.

Step 1: Capture the action as a structured record

Every meaningful step submitted to AgentLedger becomes an action record. A record captures which agent acted, what kind of action it was, the input context, the output or business result, and the agent-provided rationale. AgentLedger uses a fixed set of action types so the record shape stays consistent across platforms.

enum ActionType {
  QUERY,       // Agent reads or retrieves data
  UPDATE,      // Agent modifies existing records
  CREATE,      // Agent creates new records
  DELETE,      // Agent removes records
  DECISION,    // Agent makes a decision or selects a path
  ESCALATION,  // Agent escalates to a human operator
  TOOL_CALL,   // Agent invokes an external tool or API
  CALCULATION, // Agent performs a calculation
  VALIDATION  // Agent validates data against rules
}

The TypeScript library is deliberately simple to use. Start a session, record actions as they happen, then seal and verify it.

import { AgentLedgerSession, ActionType } from '@vluthra/agent-ledger';

const session = new AgentLedgerSession({
  agentId: 'pricing-agent',
  platform: 'salesforce',
  initiator: 'quote-workflow',
});

session.record({
  agentId: 'pricing-agent',
  actionType: ActionType.CALCULATION,
  input: { basePrice: 200, discountPct: 15 },
  output: { finalPrice: 170 },
  reasoning: 'Applied Gold tier discount to base price',
});

const sealed = session.seal();
const result = session.verify();
console.log(result.valid); // true

The field called is a recorded rationale supplied by the agent or workflow. It is not a claim that the framework captures a model’s hidden internal chain of thought. The point is to preserve the explanation the system chose to record alongside the inputs and output.

Step 2: Canonicalize before you hash

Before you can reliably hash a record, you need one consistent way to turn it into text. That's what canonicalization means. A cryptographic hash is deterministic only if the bytes going into it are deterministic. Two objects can represent the same logical information and still serialize differently because field order, missing values, dates, or formatting differ. If serialization can drift, verification becomes unreliable. AgentLedger uses the same hashing-and-sealing model in two separate implementations: the platform-agnostic TypeScript core and a implementation in Apex. In the Salesforce version, the canonicalization rule is explicit.

It builds an ordered list of fields, serializes that list as JSON, and hashes the resulting string. The order is locked:

sessionId, sequenceNumber, timestamp, agentId, actionType, inputContext, outputResult, reasoning, previousHash

The implementation also normalizes null string fields to an empty string before serialization. A missing sequence number falls back to 0. The timestamp is converted with Apex , and produces the final canonical representation.

List<String> parts = new List<String>();
parts.add(safeString(record.Audit_Session__c));
parts.add(String.valueOf(record.Sequence_Number__c != null ? record.Sequence_Number__c.intValue() : 0));
parts.add(safeString(String.valueOf(record.Action_Timestamp__c)));
parts.add(safeString(record.Agent_Id__c));
parts.add(safeString(record.Action_Type__c));
parts.add(safeString(record.Input_Context__c));
parts.add(safeString(record.Output_Result__c));
parts.add(safeString(record.Reasoning__c));
parts.add(safeString(record.Previous_Hash__c));

String canonical = JSON.serialize(parts);
return sha256(canonical);

One detail matters: the code does not arbitrarily trim the text inside input, output, or rationale fields. If someone changes whitespace inside one of those hashed fields, that is a content change and should change the hash. The deterministic part is the serialization structure, field order, and null handling.

This format becomes part of the protocol. Change the field order or serialization rules after deployment and old records will hash differently. That is why canonicalization should be versioned deliberately rather than treated as an implementation detail that can be changed casually.

Step 3: Link every record to the one before it

A cryptographic hash is essentially a fingerprint of some data. Once the canonical representation exists, AgentLedger computes a SHA-256 hash for the record and includes the previous record’s hash in the next record. In simplified form, the records form a hash-linked sequence:

Record 0: hash(content0 + null) -> H0
Record 1: hash(content1 + H0)   -> H1
Record 2: hash(content2 + H1)   -> H2

If record 1's content changes after the fact, its recomputed hash no longer matches its stored hash, so verification detects the modification. If someone also replaces record 1's stored hash with the newly computed value, record 2 still points to the original H1, so the chain linkage breaks. Rewriting one record cleanly therefore requires rewriting the downstream chain as well. The structure assumes append-only behavior, but it does not magically make the underlying database immutable.

The verifier checks more than the current record hash. It also checks that sequence numbers start at zero and increase by one with no gaps, that the first record has no previous hash, and that each later Previous Hash matches the stored hash of the preceding record.

Step 4: Seal the session under a Merkle root

A hash chain is good at showing sequence integrity. Think of the Merkle root as one fingerprint for the ordered list of record hashes in the session. Change one of those hashes and the root changes. The tree structure also lets you verify that an individual record belongs to the sealed session without supplying every other record.

             Root Hash
             /         \
         H(0,1)       H(2,3)
         /    \       /    \
       H(0)  H(1)   H(2)  H(3)

When the session is sealed, AgentLedger takes the record hashes in sequence order, hashes adjacent pairs, duplicates the last leaf when the count is odd, and repeats the process until one root remains. That root is stored as the session fingerprint.

A Merkle proof lets you verify that one record belongs to a sealed session using only the sibling hashes along its path to the root. That lets you verify one record without having to supply every other record in the session.

Verification does not ask a flag whether the session is valid. It rebuilds the evidence from the stored records and compares the result with what was sealed.

  • recompute each record hash from its current content.
  • confirm each Previous Hash matches the prior record hash and sequence numbers have no gaps.
  • rebuild the root from the record hashes and compare it with the sealed fingerprint.
  • confirm the number of records still matches the count captured for the session.

Those checks let the verifier distinguish a changed record, a broken sequence, and a count mismatch instead of returning one generic red light.

A tamper test you can reproduce

The Salesforce implementation has a simple end-to-end test that demonstrates the behavior without any special tooling:

  1. Run an agent flow that creates a session, records actions, and seals it.
  2. Click . The session shows .
  3. Edit a hashed content field on one audit record, for example the recorded rationale.
  4. Run again. The session shows because the recomputed hash no longer matches the stored hash.
  5. Restore the field to its original value.
  6. Run again. The session returns to .

That last step is important. AgentLedger proves the current record set is consistent with the sealed fingerprint. By itself, it does not prove that a temporary alteration never happened. That distinction becomes important when you talk about custody and external anchoring.

Where capture happens: move it to the boundary

There is an obvious objection to everything above. If the agent has to call itself, what stops it from simply not recording an action? A provenance trail the agent can opt out of is not worth much.

The answer is to stop relying on the agent to record itself. In the MCP reference demo, capture does not live inside the agent’s logic. It lives in middleware that wraps the MCP client’s . Every tool request routed through the gateway, and every response or error returned through it, becomes a receipt before the run continues. Declared decisions are captured at defined checkpoints the same way. For calls routed through the gateway, the agent does not choose whether to record. Recording happens because the call is on the path.

This also handles work that crosses systems. In the demo, one agent run touches five separate MCP servers, and because every call routes through the same gateway, all of it correlates into a single ordered, sealed session with one Merkle root. The record does not fragment just because the work spanned several services.

Here is the honest boundary, and it matters. Every call that routes through the gateway is captured. That is a real guarantee, and it is far stronger than hoping the agent logged itself. It is not the same as proving the agent had no other path at all. An agent given a second client or an out-of-band channel could act outside the gateway, and the receipt would not know. So the accurate claim is that every call through the capture boundary is recorded, not that every action the agent could conceivably take is recorded. Capture is enforced for calls routed through that boundary. Guaranteeing there is no path around the boundary is a deployment problem, not something the cryptography settles.

The part that is easy to get wrong: independence

Hashing does not remove the need for a trust boundary. If the records and the Merkle root live in the same system under the same privileged administrator, someone with enough access could rewrite the records, recompute the hashes, recompute the root, and leave behind a self-consistent history that is still false.

The core framework therefore gives tamper evidence against changes that are not accompanied by a full privileged rewrite. Stronger assurance requires the sealed fingerprint to leave the system that stores the records. The external anchor does not have to be a blockchain. Any independently controlled, tamper-resistant store, such as a transparency log or trusted timestamping service, could serve the same purpose.

In the reference demo, I use Arbitrum Sepolia, a public test network outside the record store that provides an independently maintained reference for the sealed root. The only AgentLedger audit payload sent outside the enterprise boundary is the 32-byte Merkle root; the underlying business data and recorded rationale remain inside.

The point is to put the fingerprint somewhere it cannot be silently rewritten along with the internal records. Anchoring addresses one specific weakness: retrospective privileged rewriting of both the records and the locally stored fingerprint. It does not solve completeness or source authenticity, and it remains a pluggable extension rather than something bundled into the core package.

What it deliberately does not prove

A provenance mechanism becomes less useful when it claims more than it can establish. These boundaries are part of the design:

  • it detects changes to records that were submitted and sealed. Capturing at the boundary, as the reference demo does, enforces recording for every call that routes through the gateway, which is a real guarantee. It still does not prove the agent had no path around the gateway, so completeness depends on how capture is deployed, not on the cryptography.
  • it protects submitted values after recording. It does not independently prove that a recorded output exactly matches the underlying business-system mutation.
  • verification proves present consistency with the fingerprint. If an altered value is later restored, the record can verify again.
  • it does not decide whether an agent was correct, unbiased, or compliant with a regulation. It preserves and verifies the recorded evidence.

This is also why I use the term rather than . The framework is built to make inconsistent changes detectable. Stronger guarantees depend on how the fingerprint is anchored and how capture is enforced.

Design constraints worth stealing

  • Zero external dependencies in the TypeScript core: hashing uses the platform crypto primitive, which keeps the verification path small.
  • identical logical inputs must map to identical bytes before hashing.
  • One model, two implementations: the TypeScript package and the Salesforce-native implementation are separate codebases that share the same hashing-and-sealing pattern.
  • in the reference demo, enforcing capture in middleware around the call, rather than trusting the agent to log itself, is the single biggest credibility gain.
  • Append-only by convention: the framework creates audit records and verifies them later rather than updating them as part of normal operation.
  • source authenticity, completeness beyond the boundary, multi-agent orchestration, and binding records to actual mutations are separate problems, stated openly rather than hidden as assumptions.

AgentLedger is open source under the MIT license. The repository includes the TypeScript core, the Salesforce implementation, the MCP gateway demo that captures across five servers and anchors a real Merkle root to a public test network, the hashing and Merkle logic, and the roadmap for the harder problems that are not solved yet.

If you run agents that make decisions that matter, try the failure path instead of trusting the happy path. Seal a session, verify it, change a recorded field, and verify again. Then look at the boundary conditions and decide what additional controls your environment needs.

items.title: AI Agents Are Becoming Employees. The Architecture of Work Has to Change
items.author: Atul Kumar
items.content:
For the last few years, much of the conversation around enterprise AI has been about whether a model is intelligent enough to answer questions, generate content, write code, summarise documents, or retrieve information from company data. That was a useful starting point, but it is becoming increasingly disconnected from what organisations are actually trying to build.

The interesting shift happens when an AI system stops being something a person talks to and starts becoming something that .

An agent might read a customer request, look up information in an internal system, call an API, create a record, send an email, update a workflow, ask another agent for information, and then continue operating without a person explicitly directing every individual step. At that point, the engineering problem changes. We are no longer designing only an AI interface. We are designing a new participant in the enterprise system.

This is where my thinking about AI architecture has changed the most through working with production-oriented AI systems. I initially looked at agents primarily through the lens of models, orchestration, retrieval, tools, context, and reliability. Over time, another question became impossible to ignore:

If an AI system can perform work inside an organisation, what exactly gives it the authority to perform that work?

That question connects almost everything else. Identity determines who the agent is. Permissions determine what it can access. Policy determines what is allowed to do. Observability determines whether we can understand what happened. Ownership determines who is responsible for operating it. Lifecycle management determines what happens when the agent changes, becomes inactive, or should no longer have access.

The model remains important, but it is no longer the entire engineering problem, and the industry is beginning to reflect that shift. Microsoft is now positioning Agent 365 as a control plane for observing, governing, and securing enterprise agents, with capabilities around agent registries, identity, access control, lifecycle management, auditing, and observability. Google Cloud's agent platform similarly includes agent identity, an agent registry, an agent gateway, governance controls, topology, and observability.[Ref]

That tells me something important: the next stage of enterprise AI is not simply about building better agents. It is about building the architecture around agents.

The moment an AI stops answering and starts acting

There is a fundamental difference between an AI assistant answering a question and an AI agent acting. Suppose an employee asks: "What is the status of this customer's order?"

The system retrieves information and produces an answer. If the answer is wrong, the immediate consequence may be a bad decision by the employee.

Now change the request: "Check the order, identify the problem, contact the customer, create a support ticket, and issue a replacement if the eligibility rules are satisfied."

That is no longer simply information retrieval; the system is now interacting with the enterprise state. It may need access to a customer database, order-management system, support platform, email service, financial rules, inventory data, and perhaps another AI service. It needs to decide which tools to call and in what order. It needs to preserve state across multiple operations. It needs to understand which actions require approval and which can happen automatically.

Most importantly, every action creates consequences. This is the point where I believe the language around "AI assistants" becomes inadequate. The architecture starts looking much more like the architecture of an organisational worker or software service than a conventional chatbot. The agent needs a recognisable identity. It needs defined responsibilities. It needs access boundaries. It needs a lifecycle. It needs monitoring. It needs an owner, and it needs a way for the organisation to say: This agent is allowed to do this, but not that.

An agent needs an organisational identity

One of the simplest mistakes an organisation can make is treating an AI agent as an anonymous process. Traditional applications already have identities. Services have service accounts. Applications have credentials. Users have accounts. Machines have identities. APIs have authentication mechanisms.

If an agent is going to perform meaningful work, it needs the same architectural treatment. Imagine an agent called customer-resolution-agent.

It might have permission to:

  • read customer support history,
  • send predefined customer communications,
  • and access specific inventory information.

It should not automatically have permission to:

  • export the entire customer database,
  • modify financial records,
  • delete customer accounts,
  • or call arbitrary external services.

The distinction is important because the agent's intelligence does not define its authority. A highly capable agent should not automatically receive highly privileged access. This is one of the areas where enterprise identity systems are now evolving. Microsoft's current Agent 365 documentation describes purpose-built agent identities and the use of Microsoft Entra controls to authenticate, authorise, monitor, and govern agents. Google Cloud similarly describes per-agent identities designed around least-privilege access and lifecycle management. [Ref]

The architecture, therefore, starts looking something like this:

                    HUMAN / BUSINESS OWNER
                              │
                              ▼
                       AGENT IDENTITY
                              │
                   ┌──────────┴──────────┐
                   │                     │
                   ▼                     ▼
                POLICY              AUTHORITY
                   │                     │
                   └──────────┬──────────┘
                              ▼
                        AI AGENT
                              │
             ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
             │                │                │
             ▼                ▼                ▼
            APIs            TOOLS             DATA
             │                │                │
             └────────────────┼────────────────┘
                              ▼
                       BUSINESS ACTION
                              │
                              ▼
                    AUDIT + OBSERVABILITY
                              │
                              ▼
                     HUMAN ACCOUNTABILITY

The important part of this architecture is not the model. It is the chain of authority surrounding the model.

Permissions are not the same thing as capability

This distinction became particularly important as I started thinking about agents as production systems rather than conversational interfaces. A model can technically call a tool without necessarily being authorised to use that tool for every situation. For example, an agent may have access to a payment API because its workflow sometimes requires payment processing. That does not mean it should be able to initiate any payment it chooses.

Capability answers: Can the system technically perform this operation?

Authorisation answers: Is the system permitted to perform this operation under these circumstances?

Those are different questions. A production architecture should therefore avoid giving an agent a large collection of unrestricted tools and trusting the model to decide when they are appropriate. Instead, the system should establish explicit boundaries. A simplified policy might look like this:

agent:
  name: customer-resolution-agent

permissions:
  read:
    - orders
    - customer_support
    - inventory

  write:
    - support_ticket
    - customer_notification

  conditional:
    replacement_order:
      requires:
        - order_status == "eligible"
        - replacement_value < 500
      approval:
        above: 500

  denied:
    - payroll
    - employee_records
    - customer_database_export

The exact implementation will vary between organisations, but the principle is broadly applicable. The model should not be the final enforcement point. The  should enforce the policy. This is also why agent gateways and centralised policy enforcement are becoming important. Google Cloud's current documentation describes Agent Gateway as a runtime enforcement point that manages agent traffic and applies access-control policies to interactions with tools and other agents [Ref]. That is a significant architectural idea, and instead of asking the model to behave correctly every time, we create infrastructure that limits what the model can actually do.

The enterprise cannot rely on the prompt as the security boundary

This is one of the lessons that became increasingly obvious to me as I worked through AI system design. A prompt can describe rules. It cannot be the only mechanism enforcing those rules. Consider an instruction such as: "Never expose confidential customer information."

That sounds reasonable, but what happens if confidential information enters the context through a document, tool response, retrieval result, or another agent?

What happens if a malicious instruction is embedded inside the retrieved content?

What happens if an external website tells the agent to perform an action that conflicts with organisational policy?

The system cannot simply assume that every piece of text entering the context is trustworthy. The architecture needs separate enforcement layers.

USER REQUEST
     │
     ▼
IDENTITY
     │
     ▼
POLICY CHECK
     │
     ▼
  AGENT
     │
     ▼
CONTEXT / RETRIEVAL
     │
     ▼
TOOL REQUEST
     │
     ▼
AUTHORIZATION
     │
     ▼
TOOL EXECUTION
     │
     ▼
RESULT VALIDATION
     │
     ▼
AUDIT + OBSERVABILITY

The model can reason about the task, but the infrastructure should decide whether the requested action is permitted. This separation becomes especially important when agents have access to systems containing sensitive business information.

Who owns an agent's decisions?

Identity solves only part of the problem. The next question is ownership. Imagine that an organisation has 500 agents.

Some were built by engineering teams. Some were created by business units. Some came from vendors. Some were developed by individual employees for internal workflows. Some are temporary experiments that became useful enough to remain in production.

Now imagine one of those agents makes an incorrect decision. Who owns it? The answer cannot simply be "the person who typed the prompt."

The organisation needs to know:

  • Who approved its deployment?
  • Who owns the business process?
  • Who approved its permissions?
  • Which version of the agent was running?
  • Which data did it access?
  • What policies were active?
  • Who is responsible when its behaviour changes?

This is why agent ownership needs to become part of architecture rather than an administrative afterthought. Microsoft's current identity-governance documentation describes human sponsorship for agent identities, including accountability for an agent's purpose, lifecycle decisions, and access reviews. [Ref]

That concept is particularly important because AI systems are not static applications. Their behaviour can change when the model changes, prompts change, retrieval changes, tools change, policies change, or the surrounding data changes.

An agent that was safe last month may behave differently after a significant update. Ownership, therefore, needs to remain active throughout the agent's lifecycle.

The new architecture of work

If agents become participants in enterprise workflows, the architecture of work starts changing. A traditional enterprise workflow might look like this:

Employee
   │
   ▼
Application
   │
   ▼
Business Process
   │
   ▼
Database / API

An agentic workflow can look more like:

Employee
   │
   ▼
AI Agent
   │
   ├────► Agent A
   │
   ├────► Agent B
   │
   ├────► Internal API
   │
   ├────► External API
   │
   ├────► Knowledge Base
   │
   └────► Enterprise Database

The number of possible interactions grows quickly. The architecture becomes a graph rather than a simple request-response pipeline, and that graph introduces new failure modes.

An agent may call another agent who calls a tool. The tool may access a database. The database may return stale information. Another agent may make a decision based on that result. Meanwhile, the underlying business state may have changed, and this is not fundamentally different from distributed systems engineering.

It is distributed systems engineering with probabilistic decision-making in the middle, and that distinction matters because many of the reliability principles we already understand become even more important.

Timeouts, Idempotency, Authorisation, Versioning, Transactions, Observability and State management matters. The AI does not remove those engineering problems. It adds another layer of complexity to them.

Why traditional RBAC is not enough by itself

Role-based access control is useful, but agents introduce situations where static roles may not provide enough context. Consider an employee who has permission to approve expenses up to ₹100,000. Should their AI agent automatically inherit the same authority? Not necessarily.

The agent may need additional constraints:

  • Which expense categories can it approve?
  • Can it approve its owner's own expenses?
  • Can it approve expenses outside business hours?
  • Can it approve recurring payments?
  • What happens if the amount exceeds a threshold?
  • What if the supporting documentation is incomplete?
  • What if the request involves a restricted vendor?

This is where authorisation starts becoming contextual. A more complete policy might consider:

WHO
  ↓
Which agent?

WHAT
  ↓
Which action?

ON WHAT
  ↓
Which resource?

UNDER WHICH CONDITIONS
  ↓
Amount, risk, data sensitivity, workflow state

FOR HOW LONG
  ↓
Time-bound authorization

WITH WHAT OVERSIGHT
  ↓
Human approval / automated policy / monitoring

This model moves beyond simply asking whether an agent belongs to a role. It asks whether a particular action is appropriate at this moment, against this resource, under these conditions. That is much closer to how high-value enterprise automation needs to work.

Not every decision should be autonomous

One of the most important architectural choices is deciding where autonomy should stop. There is a tendency in agentic AI discussions to treat human involvement as a temporary limitation. I think that is too simplistic. Human approval is not always a sign that the system failed to automate something. Sometimes it is an intentional control boundary.

For example, an agent could automatically:

  • classify an incoming request,
  • collect relevant information,
  • calculate a recommendation,
  • and create a proposed action.

But the final action might require a human when the financial, legal, security, or operational consequences cross a defined threshold. The architecture could therefore look like:

                 AI AGENT
                    │
          ┌─────────┴─────────┐
          │                   │
      LOW-RISK             HIGH-RISK
       ACTION                ACTION
          │                   │
          ▼                   ▼
    AUTOMATICALLY        HUMAN APPROVAL
       EXECUTE                │
          │                   ▼
          │              AUTHORIZED ACTION
          │                   │
          └─────────┬─────────┘
                    ▼
             AUDIT + TELEMETRY

The interesting part is that the threshold does not have to be based only on the type of action. It can also depend on uncertainty, data sensitivity, financial value, business impact, or the agent's confidence in the underlying information.

This creates a more practical definition of autonomy. Autonomy is not simply "the AI can do everything." It is the AI can operate independently within a clearly defined authority boundary.

Observability has to capture decisions, not just logs

This is another area where my view of AI observability has changed. Traditional application monitoring asks questions such as:

  • Did the API return an error?
  • How many requests failed?

Those metrics remain important, but they are insufficient for agentic systems. Imagine an agent completes a workflow successfully.

No infrastructure errors.

From a conventional monitoring dashboard, everything looks healthy. But the agent used the wrong customer record. The system may have executed exactly as designed and still produced the wrong business outcome. That means observability needs to follow the .

Request
  │
  ├── Identity
  │
  ├── Policy evaluation
  │
  ├── Model
  │
  ├── Retrieved context
  │
  ├── Tool selection
  │
  ├── Tool execution
  │
  ├── External response
  │
  ├── Agent decision
  │
  ├── Final action
  │
  └── Outcome

When something goes wrong, I want to be able to reconstruct that chain.

What information did it retrieve?

Which tool did it select?

What authorisation decision was made?

What data did the tool return?

Which model version generated the decision?

What action was finally executed?

Google Cloud's current agent platform documentation reflects this direction by connecting agent identity, gateway controls, traces, logs, metrics, topology, and evaluation. This is much closer to forensic observability than simple application monitoring.

Multiple agents create a second-order problem

One agent is already complicated. Multiple agents introduce another layer. Imagine:

                ORCHESTRATOR
                     │
        ┌────────────┼────────────┐
        ▼            ▼            ▼
    RESEARCH      FINANCE      OPERATIONS
      AGENT        AGENT          AGENT
        │            │              │
        ▼            ▼              ▼
     APIs         ERP           Inventory
        │            │              │
        └────────────┼──────────────┘
                     ▼
                FINAL ACTION

Now consider what happens when the agents have different permissions, different data sources, different versions, and different objectives.

The research agent may discover information that the finance agent is not authorised to access.

The finance agent may make a recommendation based on data that the operations agent cannot verify.

The orchestrator may combine all of these outputs without fully understanding their provenance.

The system now has an  as well as a data graph.

That is something enterprises will increasingly need to model. It is not enough to know that Agent A can call Agent B. We need to know: Why can Agent A call Agent B, under whose authority, with which permissions, using what data, and with what consequences?

That is where centralised registries and topology views become useful. Microsoft describes an agent registry and agent map for understanding agents and their connections, while Google describes centralised registries and topology graphs for agents, endpoints, and MCP servers.

Another problem I expect organisations to encounter is what I would call . Creating an agent can be remarkably easy. Managing hundreds or thousands of agents is not. An enterprise needs to think about an agent's complete lifecycle:

CREATE
  │
  ▼
REGISTER
  │
  ▼
IDENTITY
  │
  ▼
APPROVE
  │
  ▼
DEPLOY
  │
  ▼
MONITOR
  │
  ▼
REVIEW
  │
  ▼
UPDATE
  │
  ▼
SUSPEND / RETIRE

Each stage has different requirements.

During creation, the organisation needs to understand the purpose of the agent. During registration, it needs to establish identity and ownership. Before deployment, permissions and policies need to be evaluated. During operation, behaviour and performance need to be monitored. During updates, changes to models, tools, prompts, policies, or data dependencies need to be evaluated.

When the agent is retired, its credentials and access need to be revoked. This may sound like ordinary application lifecycle management. But the difference is that agent behaviour is often more dynamic. An agent can adapt its path through a workflow based on context. That makes lifecycle governance especially important.

Microsoft's current Agent 365 architecture explicitly includes lifecycle management, including controls around inactive, ownerless, and risky agents.[Ref]

This is probably the architectural conclusion I keep coming back to. For years, we focused on the application. Then we built platforms around applications. Now we are starting to need platforms around agents. The architecture begins to look like:

                 ┌───────────────────────────────┐
                 │        AGENT CONTROL PLANE    │
                 │                               │
                 │ Identity                      │
                 │ Policy                        │
                 │ Registry                      │
                 │ Permissions                   │
                 │ Security                      │
                 │ Observability                 │
                 │ Audit                         │
                 │ Lifecycle                     │
                 │ Evaluation                    │
                 │ Cost                          │
                 └───────────────┬───────────────┘
                                 │
               ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
               │                 │                 │
               ▼                 ▼                 ▼
            Agent A           Agent B           Agent C
               │                 │                 │
               └─────────────────┼─────────────────┘
                                 │
                    ┌────────────┼────────────┐
                    ▼            ▼            ▼
                  APIs         Data          Tools
                    │            │            │
                    └────────────┼────────────┘
                                 ▼
                       ENTERPRISE SYSTEMS

The control plane does not replace the agents. It makes them manageable, and that distinction is important.

I don't think the future enterprise will have one giant AI system making every decision. It is more likely to have many specialised agents operating within different business processes, connected to different systems, with different authorities and responsibilities. The challenge will therefore be coordinating them without losing visibility or control.

What I would design differently today

If I were designing a production AI agent architecture today, I would start with the authority model before starting with the prompt. I would first define what the agent is responsible for and what it is explicitly not responsible for. I would give it an identifiable owner and a dedicated identity. I would define the resources it can access and make those permissions as narrow as practical.

Then I would design the workflow around policy enforcement rather than trusting the model to follow instructions. The model would be responsible for reasoning and selecting appropriate actions within the available capabilities. The infrastructure would remain responsible for authentication, authorisation, policy enforcement, validation, auditing, and execution boundaries.

I would also make observability part of the architecture from the beginning rather than adding dashboards after deployment. For every meaningful action, I would want to answer:

Who initiated this?
Which agent acted?
Which identity did it use?
What context did it receive?
Which policy applied?
Which tools were called?
What data was accessed?
What decision was produced?
What action was executed?
What was the outcome?

If those questions cannot be answered, the system is not yet operationally mature enough for high-impact autonomous work. I would also separate low-risk automation from high-impact actions and establish explicit approval boundaries. Finally, I would treat agents as lifecycle-managed infrastructure rather than permanent scripts.

An agent should have a creation date, owner, version, identity, permissions, dependencies, monitoring, review process, and retirement mechanism. That sounds less exciting than talking about autonomous intelligence. But in production, these details are where reliability comes from.

The enterprise will have to manage AI differently

The more I work through these architectures, the less I think the central question is whether AI agents will replace particular categories of software or workers. The more immediate engineering question is how organisations will integrate systems that can reason, use tools, maintain state, and perform actions into environments that were designed around predictable software and accountable humans. That requires a change in architecture.

An employee, an application, and a service have an identity.

An AI agent that can access enterprise systems should not be treated as an exception. It should have one too.

An employee, application, or service has permissions.

Agents need permissions that are explicit, scoped, reviewable, and revocable.

Employees, applications operate within organisational policies.

Agents need policy boundaries that are enforceable by infrastructure rather than merely described in prompts, and when something goes wrong, an organisation needs to reconstruct what happened. That means identity, policy, observability, and auditability cannot remain separate concerns. They become part of the AI architecture itself.

AI agents are not just another software feature

This is probably the biggest lesson I have taken from working on production-oriented AI systems. When an AI system only generates text, the architecture can often hide a lot of complexity behind an interface.

Once the AI starts acting, that complexity becomes visible. The system needs to understand the state.

It needs to manage context, authenticate, authorise, call tools, handle failures, deal with changing data, produce traceable decisions, respect organisational policies and answer a very human question: Who is accountable for what it did?

That is why I think the next phase of enterprise AI engineering will be less about building increasingly impressive demonstrations and more about building the infrastructure that makes autonomous systems trustworthy enough to operate continuously.

The model will continue to improve, the agents will become more capable, the number of tools available to them will increase, and organisations will deploy more of them. But capability without an authority model creates a system that can act without a sufficiently clear understanding of where its authority begins and ends.

The real engineering opportunity is therefore not simply to create agents that can do more. It is to create enterprises where agents can do the right amount of work, with the right authority, under the right policies, with the right level of oversight.

That is a much harder problem than building another chatbot, and, in my view, it is also where some of the most interesting AI engineering work is beginning.

Putting the entire idea together, the architecture I would use as a mental model is:

                         ┌─────────────────────┐
                         │   BUSINESS OWNER    │
                         └──────────┬──────────┘
                                    │
                                    ▼
                         ┌─────────────────────┐
                         │   AGENT IDENTITY    │
                         │ Owner / Sponsor     │
                         │ Credentials        │
                         └──────────┬──────────┘
                                    │
                    ┌───────────────┼────────────────┐
                    ▼               ▼                ▼
               ┌─────────┐    ┌──────────┐     ┌───────────┐
               │ POLICY  │    │ PERMISSION│     │ LIFECYCLE │
               │ ENGINE  │    │  ENGINE   │     │ MANAGEMENT│
               └────┬────┘    └────┬─────┘     └─────┬─────┘
                    │              │                 │
                    └──────────────┼─────────────────┘
                                   ▼
                         ┌─────────────────────┐
                         │      AI AGENT       │
                         │ Reasoning / Planning│
                         │ Context / Memory    │
                         └──────────┬──────────┘
                                    │
                  ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
                  ▼                 ▼                 ▼
              ┌───────┐         ┌───────┐         ┌───────┐
              │ TOOLS │         │ APIs  │         │ DATA  │
              └───┬───┘         └───┬───┘         └───┬───┘
                  │                 │                 │
                  └─────────────────┼─────────────────┘
                                    ▼
                         ┌─────────────────────┐
                         │ EXECUTION BOUNDARY  │
                         │ Validation / Policy │
                         │ Approval / Controls │
                         └──────────┬──────────┘
                                    │
                                    ▼
                         ┌─────────────────────┐
                         │ BUSINESS ACTION     │
                         └──────────┬──────────┘
                                    │
                                    ▼
              ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
              │       OBSERVABILITY + AUDIT             │
              │ Traces | Decisions | Tools | Data       │
              │ Policies | Outcomes | Cost | Errors     │
              └─────────────────────────────────────────┘

The architectural shift is straightforward to describe but difficult to implement: the agent should not be the control plane. The agent operates inside the control plane, and as AI moves deeper into enterprise workflows, that distinction may become one of the most important design principles in AI engineering.

items.title: How to Add Text to AI-Generated Video Without It Looking Broken
items.author: Frank Houbre
items.content:
The first title card I generated for Lost Garden came back covered in letters that weren’t in any alphabet. Not a typo, not a font issue. The model had understood I wanted text and then drawn something that was confidently, beautifully, not a word. I regenerated it a few more times. One pass fixed a line and broke another. Eventually I gave up and did what I should have done from the start: I made the card somewhere else.

If you want readable text in an AI-generated film, the answer is almost never to get the video model to write it. You generate the image without any words in it, then add the real text as a layer afterward, in an actual editor. That one sentence is the whole workaround, and once you know it, it changes how you plan every title card, sign and on-screen note in the project.

This is not a complaint about the models. They were never trained to spell, they were trained to make convincing pixels, and convincing pixels and correct letterforms are two different skills that happen to look similar from a distance. Knowing that changes what you ask them to do.

Why can’t AI video models render readable text?

A video diffusion model predicts what a frame should plausibly look like, not what a sentence should correctly say. Letters are small, dense, high-frequency shapes, and the model has no concept of spelling, it only has a concept of “text-shaped marks in this kind of composition.” That’s why you get something that reads as a sign from across the street and turns into static the moment you get close enough to try reading it.

Static image models handle targeted edits far better than video models handle text in motion.
