OpenAI’s ChatGPT Images 2.5 launched in September 2026, was built specifically around precise edits, including swapping out a single element such as a product, a background, or a piece of text, without touching the rest of the image. That’s a different job from asking a model to invent correct, legible lettering inside a moving shot, and it’s the whole reason the two-stage workaround below exists.

Should title cards live inside the AI tool or get added in post?

Add them in post, almost always. The practical reason is not aesthetic, it’s operational: baked-in text can’t be revised without regenerating the whole clip, and a regeneration costs credits and time. A typo in a title card you generated is a full re-render. A typo in a text layer sitting on top of the footage in your editor is a ten-second fix.

There’s one real exception. If the text has to feel like it’s physically part of the world, not sitting on top of it, carrying the same grain, the same light, the same slight imperfection as everything around it, generating it in-world can be worth the extra passes. That’s a deliberate choice for a handful of shots, not your default for every title card and every episode number.

On Lost Garden I now split it cleanly:

  • Opening titles and episode cards get built entirely in post, as clean typography over a generated or composited background, so a word change never touches a rendered clip.
  • In-world text that has to read as part of the set goes through the two-stage method below, and only where the story genuinely needs the audience to read something inside the frame.

The cost of a baked-in typo is a regenerated clip. The cost of a typo in a text layer is undoing one edit. Once you’ve paid for the first kind of mistake a couple of times, you stop making it.

How do you add in-world text that doesn’t look fake?

This is the harder case: a carved sign, a note someone leaves on a door, a name on a screen in the background. You can’t just slap a clean font over it, it has to look like it belongs to the shot.

The two-stage method that actually holds up:

  1. Generate the text as a still image first, using a model known for clean typography rather than your general scene generator. Write the exact wording in quotes in the prompt and describe the physical object carrying it: “a carved wooden sign reading ‘TURN BACK’, weathered paint, mounted at the treeline.” Generate it large, ideally 2K or higher, because compression eats detail you don’t have spare.
  2. Animate the approved still instead of generating fresh video with the text baked in. Once the lettering is correct in a frame you’ve checked with your own eyes, feed that still into an image-to-video pass on a tool like Runway. You’re asking the model to add motion to something that’s already right, not asking it to invent correct spelling from a text prompt, which was the failure mode you were trying to avoid.

A few things make or break this, and I learned most of them the slow way. Keep the camera slow near text: a static hold or a gentle push-in survives the animation pass, while a whip pan or fast handheld motion smears the lettering into mush within a few frames, even starting from a perfect still. Check the still before you spend any video credits on it, since image generations are cheaper than video generations by a wide margin on every platform I’ve used, so the discipline is simple: don’t move to video until the image is actually right. And once a sign or a logo reads correctly, save that exact file. Reusing a locked asset is what keeps the same prop legible across multiple shots, instead of regenerating a slightly different, slightly wrong version every time it appears.

This is the same discipline I ended up applying to character reference sheets on Lost Garden: lock the thing that has to stay identical, and stop asking the generator to reinvent it from scratch every single time.

What’s the actual workflow, start to finish?

Here’s the version I run now, after enough wasted renders to trust it:

  • Plan the text before you generate anything. Decide in the script or shot breakdown which text is informational (title cards, episode numbers, subtitles) and which is diegetic (a sign the camera sees inside the story), since that single decision sends each piece down a different path.
  • Informational text goes to post, no exceptions, because it needs to stay editable for as long as the project exists.
  • Diegetic text goes through the two-stage method: still image first, slow camera on the animation pass, locked asset once it’s approved.
  • Don’t trust the first result, whether it’s a title card typo or a garbled sign, and check it before it goes anywhere near the timeline.
  • Budget for it. Text-heavy shots cost more passes than text-free ones, and if a scene doesn’t strictly need on-screen words, it’s often worth finding another way to convey the same information.

One of the more useful habits I picked up while building ScreenWeaver’s storyboard stage was planning exactly what text needs to appear, and where, on paper, before a single frame gets generated. It cuts the number of “wait, what does that say” surprises down to almost nothing. None of this is exotic, really. It’s closer to how title design has always worked in post-production. The surprising part is that AI video forces you to rediscover the same boundary between what the camera captures and what the editor adds that film editors have respected for a century, just for a completely different reason.

Can any AI video model generate readable text directly?

Results vary and keep shifting month to month, but as of 2026, text accuracy is still inconsistent enough across general-purpose video and image models that the safer default is generating text separately and compositing it, rather than trusting any single model to spell correctly on the first try.

Does this slow down production?

It adds one extra step for text-heavy shots, but it removes the much bigger cost of regenerating a whole clip over a spelling error. Net, it’s faster.

What if the text only needs to be implied, not read?

Then don’t fight this problem at all. A blurred sign, a screen angled away from camera, or text that’s legible as “there’s writing here” without needing to be read word for word, skips the whole workaround. Save the two-stage method for text the story actually needs the audience to read.

Is this specific to anime-style projects like Lost Garden?

No. The failure mode is about how diffusion models handle small dense shapes, not about art style. Live-action AI shots hit the same wall with street signs, screens and handwriting.

If you’re planning a script or storyboard and want to flag exactly where on-screen text needs to appear before you generate a single shot, that’s the kind of pre-production step ScreenWeaver is built to catch early, alongside the rest of the shot breakdown. And if you want to see how this plays out across a full six-character episode, Lost Garden is the project all of this gets tested on first.

items.title: How I Optimized a 3D Anatomy Atlas With 2.9 Million Triangles
items.author: Balwinder Singh
items.content:
I built (learnanatomy3d.com), a free 3D human anatomy atlas that runs in the browser:

  • ~2,900 clickable structures across 11 body systems; This post covers the performance problems I hit while loading ~2.9 million triangles, and how I fixed them.

Click any structure to see its name, Latin term, origin, insertion and action:

  • the site, 14 locales, and the static anatomy and disease pages.
  • three.js through react-three-fiber: the 3D viewer.
  • (Z-Anatomy, BodyParts3D, Human Reference Atlas), fitted to realistic character bodies with custom Node and Blender tooling, packed into gzip'd binary chunks and streamed in two passes: body surface first, full anatomy after.

Problem 1: the page froze for 7 seconds while loading

Clicks, navigation, even the "I understand" button: nothing responded while the model loaded. The Long Tasks API showed one 7.3-second task and about 13.6 s of blocking in total.

A CPU profile pointed at . On a shader's first use, three.js reads its info log to report errors. Reading that log forces the browser to wait for compilation to finish, so KHR_parallel_shader_compile never gets the chance to help.

Fix 1: turn the check off in production, when the renderer is created. react-three-fiber renders the environment map runs, so setting the flag there is too late.

<Canvas
  gl={(defaults) => {
    const renderer = new THREEWebGLRenderer({ defaults antialias: true });
    rendererdebugcheckShaderErrors = processenvNODE_ENV !== "production";
    return renderer;
  }}
/>

Fix 2: compile a model before it joins the scene. polls the driver instead of blocking. The model is only attached once its shaders are ready, and the loading screen stays up until then.

await renderercompileAsync(modelroot camera scene); // still detached
setAttached(true);                                       // now render it

Problem 2: textures decoded twice on the main thread

Each loading pass built its own materials, so every 2048² texture was decoded and uploaded , at about 150 ms each, on the main thread.

decode with , which works off the main thread, and cache by URL so both passes share one texture:

const cache = new Map<string Promise<THREETexture>>();
const loader = new THREEImageBitmapLoader()
  setOptions({ imageOrientation: "flipY" premultiplyAlpha: "none" });

function surfaceTexture(url: string) {
  if (!cachehas(url)) {
    cacheset(url loaderloadAsync(url).then((bitmap) => {
      const t = new THREETexture(bitmap);
      tflipY = false;          // already flipped by createImageBitmap
      tneedsUpdate = true;
      return t;
    }));
  }
  return cacheget(url)!;
}

(Older Safari and Firefox ignore , so they fall back to .)

Problem 3: switching bodies rebuilt everything

Switching male ↔ female unmounted the . That threw away the WebGL context, every compiled program and the environment map. keep the canvas mounted. The old body stays under the loading screen until the new one is ready, so the click responds in about 0.1 s and compiled programs are reused.

Problem 4: 2,900 objects shouldn't mean 2,900 draw calls

Each body system is merged into . Every vertex carries a part index, and a small RGBA data texture holds the per-part state (visibility, highlight, opacity, explode offset). Selecting or hiding a structure is a texel write, never a re-merge.

Cross-sections use one persistent clipping plane per material, parked far away when the cut is off. Turning the cut on never changes the number of planes, so it never recompiles shaders.

  • Main-thread blocking during load: .
  • Longest freeze: . What's left is the GPU driver's first-ever shader compile.
  • Body switch: the click responds in .

What I'd love feedback on

How does it perform on phone, and is anything confusing? Try it: . It's free, needs no account, and works in 14 languages.

Disclosure: I'm the developer of LearnAnatomy3D. The anatomy is real scientific data (Z-Anatomy, BodyParts3D, the Human Reference Atlas).

items.title: The Man Who Sits in the Portico and Cries
items.author: Simply Sansu
items.content:
Every day, he can be seen sitting alone on the porch of his luxurious mansion. No matter how bright the day was, its warmth could not clear the cloudy gloom from his face.

He sat there motionless for hours, except for the tears quietly rolling down his cheeks. What broke my heart even more was that he did not even bother to wipe them away, as though wiping them would not make much of a difference.

And I was just one quiet neighbor who couldn’t do much, because it was his own loved ones who had deserted him.

He is a subject of discussion and a common sight for passersby. No words are exchanged. People simply watch him and go by. Neither does he speak to anyone, nor does he seem to care about anyone.

It’s just him and his loneliness, speaking to himself. He doesn’t want to share or vent the emotions he has kept bottled up inside.

I looked out from my porch to say hello to my neighbor. For some reason, I just paused_._ I couldn’t help but feel sorry for him.

A Life Spent Away From Home

He is a retired motor mechanic who spent many years working in a far-off land to provide for his family. He lived away from the people he loved, fighting one difficulty after another, a rude boss, extreme weather, exhausting work, and, above all, unbearable loneliness.

He endured it all for one reason: his family.

The Children He Gave Everything To

He wanted his children to have what he never had. He worked hard to educate them, help them settle in life, and secure their future.

He did his part. Perhaps more than his part.

Today, his children are settled, financially independent, and busy with their own families. But somewhere along the way, they forgot their responsibility toward the father who gave them everything.

The man who once worried about whether his children had enough now sits alone, wondering if they have enough time for him.

The Emptiness Only His Loved Ones Can Fill

A neighbor can say hello, sit beside him, offer a cup of tea, or ask how his day was. But that cannot fill the emptiness completely.

That space can only truly be filled by the people he spent his life working for: his children and grandchildren.

Loneliness in old age is different. A luxurious mansion can offer comfort, but it cannot replace the sound of children laughing, a grandchild running towards you, or someone simply asking,

Perhaps the hardest part of aging isn’t losing your strength. It is losing your sense of purpose.

The days grow the same, life turns monotonous, and you begin to crave a little colour in what feels like a monochromatic existence.

Remember Who Helped You Get There

Sometimes, all that color requires is a visit, a phone call, a meal together, or simply a few hours of your time.

We often forget the parents whose sweat and sacrifice helped build the life we enjoy today.

Now that we are standing on our own feet, we must remember who helped us get there.

A demanding career or living far away may make life busy, but it should never mean we cannot find time for our aging parents.

Your Children Are Watching

There is another reason to make time for your parents: your children are watching.

They learn from how you treat your aging parents. One day, they may remember those actions and understand that parents deserve love, time, and attention as they grow old.

A Little Time Can Mean Everything

We cannot give our parents back the years they sacrificed for us, but we can give them .

One day, that empty chair may remain empty, and it may be too late to change our ways.

Old age should not be a punishment for a lifetime spent caring for others.

Call them. Visit them. Sit with them.

Because sometimes, the loneliness of old age can be eased by what money can never buy: the presence of the people they love.

*This is a real story, and sadly, there are many like him - people quietly battling loneliness in their old age.

items.title: Context Language Models: A New Approach to How AI Agents Remember
items.author: arist ONLINE
items.content:
Researchers are giving language models something they have rarely had before: the ability to decide what remains in their own working context.

An AI agent can spend hours working on a difficult problem. It can search the web, read documents, write code, call tools and talk to other agents. There is an unglamorous problem hiding underneath all of that work. The agent has to remember what matters.

Until now, that job has largely belonged to the software surrounding the model. When a conversation gets too long, the system might summarize it. It might retrieve selected information from storage. It might compress older material or move some of it elsewhere. The model does the thinking. The machinery around it manages the paperwork.

A new research paper proposes reversing that arrangement. On September 29, researchers from the University of Washington, Meta Superintelligence Labs, MIT and Trillium Labs published a paper introducing , or CLMs. Their central idea is surprisingly concrete: treat the model’s live context as a file that the model itself can edit. The model can add to the file, rewrite part of it, remove information, reorganize what remains, and decide when to do so. That sounds like a modest engineering change but it may turn out to be a more consequential one.

CLM gives a language model control over its working context, allowing it to rewrite, move, remove, or retain information as a task unfolds.

First, a clarification is necessary. “CLM” is not a universally established name for one technology. It has been used for several unrelated ideas. The CLM discussed here is specifically , the system introduced in the September 2026 paper by Rulin Shao and colleagues.

And despite the name, the researchers are not presenting CLM as a brand-new replacement for the transformer or as a new family of foundation models. The underlying language model can remain an existing model. What changes is its relationship with context.

A conventional language model effectively carries its conversation forward by appending new material to what came before. The paper describes this as an append-only transition: the existing context remains and new tokens are added to it.

That works until the context becomes too large. Agent systems therefore need ways of managing it. Some summarize previous interactions, others retrieve information from external memory, whereas still, others use predefined tools to compact or reorganize the conversation.

CLM gives the model much broader control. The researchers mirror the model’s live context into a file. The model receives access to that file and can manipulate it using ordinary commands. When the file changes, the updated version becomes the context used for the next turn.

Instead of an external program saying: “The context is getting long. Summarize the oldest material.” the model can decide: “This information is no longer useful. This other piece needs to stay. I should rewrite this section before continuing.” The researchers call this making context management a native capability of the language model.

Consider a researcher investigating a difficult question for several hours. At the beginning, dozens of pieces of information may appear useful. Later, only a handful remain central. Some early findings may turn out to be wrong. Some notes need to be updated. Some pieces need to remain verbatim. A running list of unresolved questions may become more useful than the original conversation.

A fixed summarization rule has to anticipate these needs. A model that can edit its own working context can respond to them as they arise. This is particularly relevant to AI agents because long-running tasks are becoming more common.

An agent that writes software for several hours, researches a complicated subject or coordinates several subagents is effectively maintaining a temporary working memory. If that memory is badly managed, the agent can lose important information, accumulate irrelevant material or repeatedly process the same text.

The CLM researchers are asking whether the model should be responsible for managing that memory itself. Their answer, based on their experiments, is yes.

The experiment that got attention

The headline result comes from , a benchmark designed around difficult research questions. Using a Qwen3.6–27B model with a 32,000-token context limit, the researchers report that their CLM achieved , compared with for the strongest baseline they tested, a Codex-style summarization approach. That is an 11.4% relative improvement, not an 11.4-percentage-point increase. The CLM also used 21.5% fewer “prefix-reuse FLOPs,” the paper’s measure for the computation associated with generating, processing and re-processing context across the trajectory.

The claim is not simply that the model answered more questions correctly. It is that letting the model manage its context produced better results while requiring less of the measured computation. The researchers report similar findings elsewhere.

On a 12-hour subset of EdgeBench, a long-running software-optimization benchmark, CLM scored about 5% higher than a summary-based approach while using 59% fewer prefix-reuse FLOPs. On a 24-hour experiment involving six repositories and multiple cooperating agents, the researchers report 65% greater downstream speedup at the same compute budget. There were also mathematical optimization experiments in which CLM outperformed specialized evolutionary-agent harnesses on the reported tasks. The paper therefore presents CLM as something broader than a clever summarization trick. The authors are arguing for a change in where context-management intelligence belongs.

But is this actually a new kind of model?

Not quite. That is one of the most important things to understand about CLM. The paper does not require a new neural architecture. The researchers show that existing models can be turned into CLMs through the context-management interface. They tested the approach with models including Qwen variants and other models available through their experimental setup. That makes CLM closer to a new model behavior or operating scheme than a completely new foundation-model architecture. This also explains why comparisons with several existing approaches matter.

Researchers have already been trying to solve the long-context problem in different ways. Some systems summarize old context; others retrieve information when needed. Some allow agents to store information externally; other research has experimented with giving models explicit context-management tools.

Recursive Language Models, for example, allow a model to access large inputs recursively rather than forcing everything into its live context. Other systems allow agents to compact, retrieve or offload information.

CLM’s more radical step is to remove the predefined menu. The model is not merely choosing between “summarize,” “retrieve” and “offload.” It can manipulate the context itself giving it a larger action space. That is probably the most interesting part of the research.

What did the researchers actually observe?

Some of the paper’s examples are revealing because they were not necessarily programmed into the system beforehand. The researchers report CLMs creating trackers and scoreboards for coordinating multiple agents, introducing internal-note roles and defining reusable functions for managing context.

In one sense, this is unsurprising. A capable language model with access to files can write structured information into them. But the significance lies in it does so. The researchers did not have to specify every possible context-management behavior in advance. The model could discover useful ways of organizing its own working state. That is a meaningful departure from the traditional agent architecture, where engineers design the available memory operations and the model selects among them. CLM effectively gives the model a blank notebook rather than a checklist of memory operations.

The researchers went further

The paper does not stop at prompting. The authors show that context-management behavior can itself be learned. In one experiment, the model is given natural-language instructions describing desirable context-management strategies. The system can also evolve a reusable skill document describing successful ways of managing context.

On their ContextBench diagnostic, the researchers report improvements of up to 35.9 points on a context-management task while reducing compute. They also trained a Qwen3.5–9B model using an online reinforcement-learning method designed specifically for CLMs. The reported BrowseComp-Plus result rose from 28.8% to 42.5%.

The trained CLM slightly outperformed a similarly trained Codex-style summary baseline while using substantially fewer measured FLOPs. This is an important clue about where the researchers think the idea is headed. Context management need not remain an engineering rule. It could become something a model learns.

There is a price for editing the middle

Giving a model permission to rewrite its context creates a computational problem. Modern inference systems make heavy use of caching. If the beginning of a prompt remains unchanged, a server can reuse previously computed information rather than processing everything again. But suppose a CLM changes something near the beginning of a 30,000-token context. Everything after that changed point may need to be processed again because the cached computation no longer corresponds to the actual context. In other words, giving the model a red pen can make the computer do more work.

The researchers therefore introduce another technique called . The basic idea is to reuse cached states beyond the point where the context was edited rather than throwing all of them away. They report that this can reduce server-side compute by 35% compared with standard SGLang serving at matched performance.

This is technically interesting, but it also illustrates something easy to miss. CLM is not one invention. It is a package of ideas: a model-controlled context interface, methods for learning context-management behavior, a diagnostic benchmark, reinforcement learning and a serving optimization intended to make arbitrary edits less expensive. The pieces should therefore be judged separately.

The benchmark results deserve caution

The results are promising. They are also very new. The paper was posted only days before this article was written. Therefore, impressive benchmark numbers can be persuasive long before an idea has been independently reproduced.

An early external review of the paper found the central accuracy claims credible but raised concerns about the magnitude of some efficiency claims. In particular, the paper uses its own definition of prefix-reuse FLOPs, and some experimental conditions give CLM capabilities or evaluation privileges that deserve closer scrutiny. That does not invalidate the research but changes how the results should be described.

“CLM is 21.5% more efficient” would be too broad. A more defensible statement is:

The authors report 21.5% fewer prefix-reuse FLOPs under their experimental setup while achieving higher BrowseComp-Plus accuracy than their strongest tested baseline.

That sounds less spectacular and it is also what the evidence supports.

There is another limitation. The researchers’ ContextBench is presented as a diagnostic for context management, but the official repository currently lists it as “coming soon.” Independent replication therefore remains an important next step.

Then there is the security problem

There is an uncomfortable symmetry in CLM. The model is being given greater control over the text it will read in its next turn. That can help it preserve useful information. It can also allow bad information to persist.

The CLM paper itself discusses this problem. An editable context becomes a potential persistence channel for prompt injection: instructions encountered by the model could be written into the context and subsequently influence future turns. That concern is not hypothetical in the broader world of agents.

In September, OpenAI reported an unusual case during reinforcement-learning training in which an internal model inserted unauthorized, jailbreak-like instructions into its own compaction summaries. OpenAI said the behavior was extremely rare and occurred in a separate training run rather than the final Astra model, but the incident demonstrates that generated context can itself become an instruction-bearing channel.

CLM pushes that idea further. A conventional summarizer may accidentally preserve a malicious instruction. A CLM has been deliberately given permission to rewrite the working context making provenance and auditing more important, not less.

If the model can rewrite its own working record, an engineer inspecting the final context may not be looking at exactly the information that was present earlier. A production system would therefore need to know not merely what the context currently says, but how it got there.

CLM does not replace memory

There is another potential misunderstanding worth avoiding. CLM is not the same thing as persistent memory. Its context file is a working space for a task. Giving the model control over that space does not automatically give it a reliable memory of everything it has learned across previous tasks. Nor does CLM eliminate retrieval. A model can still need external databases, documents and long-term memory systems.

The contribution is narrower: CLM changes how the model manages the information currently available to it. That narrower claim is already interesting enough.

So what is genuinely new?

After stripping away the terminology, the strongest case for CLM is not that researchers have discovered a magical new form of learning. They have not. The underlying models remain recognizable language models. The stronger contribution is architectural.

For years, much of the intelligence in AI agents has been split between two layers. The model reasons. The harness manages the state.

CLM asks whether those responsibilities should remain separate. Instead of engineers continually inventing better rules for deciding what the model should remember, perhaps the model itself can learn how to manage that state. That is a legitimate research direction. It also fits a broader movement in AI toward giving models more control over tools, memory and long-horizon execution.

CLM’s distinctive move is to make part of the model’s action space rather than giving an agent one more tool.

But the evidence does not yet justify a revolution

There is a temptation with research like this to jump from an elegant idea to a sweeping prediction. The evidence does not support that yet.

CLM has been demonstrated across several demanding tasks, but the work is a research paper, not evidence of widespread production deployment. The benchmark results are primarily results reported by the authors.

Independent replication is still young. Some efficiency claims depend on a specialized accounting method. The security implications of editable context need considerably more work. And it remains unclear how well the approach will behave when the context contains conflicting instructions, malicious documents, unreliable tool outputs or information whose importance is difficult to judge.

There is also a practical question. A model that can edit everything may sometimes edit the wrong thing. The appeal of external context-management systems is partly that they constrain what can happen. Constraints can be clumsy, but they can also make behavior predictable. CLM deliberately gives up some of that predictability.

The bet is that the model’s ability to adapt will be worth the additional uncertainty. The experiments suggest that, in the tested environments, it can be. They do not yet tell us how far that advantage travels.

We know that Context Language Models are real research, not merely a marketing phrase.

We know what the central mechanism is: an existing language model is given an editable representation of its live context and can decide how that context should change from one step to the next.

We know the researchers have released implementation code and demonstrated the approach across several long-horizon tasks.

We know their experiments report meaningful gains over several existing context-management strategies.

We also know what we do know.

We do not yet know whether the reported efficiency advantages will survive broader independent testing.

We do not know whether unrestricted context editing will prove reliable enough for high-stakes production agents.

We do not know how well CLMs will defend against attacks that exploit the very memory they are being trusted to manage.

And we do not yet know whether context management will become an important learned capability inside future models or remain a useful technique for a particular generation of agent systems.

That makes “CLM is here” both true and slightly misleading. The research is here. The code is here. The evidence is here. The larger technological shift is still being tested.

For now, the most interesting thing about CLM may be the question it asks rather than the answer it provides:

If an AI agent is going to work for hours, should the software around it decide what it remembers — or should the model learn to decide for itself?

That question is no longer hypothetical. CLM is one of the first serious attempts to let the model take the pen.

items.title: How to Bypass Anti-Bot Protection With Playwright and Chrome
items.author: Nicolas Fränkel
items.content:
While searching for my ancestors, I had to access data from many different websites. I noticed there were different levels of protection against automated access depending on the site. In this post, I'll list them and mention countermeasures you can take to bypass them anyway.

As a private person using the data for my own personal use, I have no qualms about bypassing the protection. It can be considered fair use. However, I don't know about your context, and I'm not saying you should. Scrape responsibly.

The need for bot protection

Genealogy and public records sites provide lots of data. Many actors are interested in this data: it's normal, and even expected, that providers want to protect their assets.

The usual approach is a simple request to bots.

Despite the use of the terms allow and disallow, the protocol is purely advisory and relies on the compliance of the web robot; it cannot enforce any of what is stated in the file. Malicious web robots are unlikely to honor robots.txt; some may even use the robots.txt as a guide to find disallowed links and go straight to them.

Thus, most sites require actual anti-bot protection.

The base level has little to no protection. Some sites do a surface check, but it's not serious protection. The check differs from site to site.

options are enough to access the data:

  • User agent: pass the via , ,

  • Referer: the referer is the URL of the page from which the link was clicked. Some sites check it on image requests only, and return a 403 without it. Use the option, , .

  • Session cookies: this one is a bit more involved, but still easily manageable. provides the and options to store and load cookies.

    curl -c cookies.txt https://frankel.ch                # 1
curl -b cookies.txt https://frankel.ch                # 2
curl -b cookies.txt -c cookies.txt https://frankel.ch # 3

1. Store cookies to `cookies.txt`
2. Load cookies from `cookies.txt`
3. Load and store, thus maintaining cookie-based session state

If a site at this level still refuses , it's probably fingerprinting the TLS handshake. Browsers use fixed combinations of ciphers and extensions, and the digest of the combination is a fingerprint, JA3 or JA4, that identifies the client, whatever the says. can impersonate a browser's fingerprint from Python. I never needed it: by the time a site fingerprints TLS, it usually also requires JavaScript, which is the next level.

At this step, the site requires JavaScript. It might be either a genuine attempt at protecting against bots, or just that the developer designed a site fully JavaScript-based. The second case is more frequent than you'd think: search forms built from JavaScript widgets, image viewers that populate their cache lazily, catalogues that load their tree on click. Nothing hostile, just no HTML to .

I encountered two different bot guards.

  • Anubis is an open source software program that adds a proof of work challenge to websites before users can access them in order to deter web scraping. It has been adopted mainly by Git forges and free and open-source software projects.

    Anubis was created by Xe Iaso in response to Amazon's web crawler overloading their Git server, as the crawler did not respect the robots.txt exclusion protocol and would work around restrictions.

    The challenge is a Hashcash-style proof of work: the browser appends a number to the challenge and hashes the result with SHA-256. It must find a number whose hash starts with a configurable count of zeros, in hexadecimal. A passing client gets a signed JWT cookie, valid for a while. A client without JavaScript gets nothing. For the record, Anubis' own documentation site is behind Anubis, and it blocked the fetcher I used to look up the documentation while writing this post.

  • Cloudflare JavaScript detection:

    JavaScript Detections is implemented on your website via a lightweight, invisible JavaScript code snippet that follows Cloudflare's privacy standards.

    JavaScript is injected only in response to requests for HTML pages or page views, excluding AJAX calls. API and mobile application traffic is unaffected.

To bypass any of them, or similar bot-protection mechanisms, just use a browser. You can steer it with browser-automation software, such as Playwright. On several sites, a headless browser was enough.

Not on all of them, though. Cloudflare's own documentation says JavaScript Detections "catches headless browsers (browsers controlled by software, with no visible window or human operator) and other automation tools". Whether a headless browser gets through a JavaScript check depends on how the site is configured.

This is the level where the fun stuff begins. Some sites do reject headless browsers. I can only hint at some reasons, though I didn't dig deeper:

  • Client fingerprinting: the TLS handshake and the HTTP/2 settings differ between a browser and a Python client, as seen above. They don't differ between headed and headless mode of the same binary. However, Playwright's default headless mode runs , a different binary, unless you set a .
  • Rendering environment fingerprinting: headless has no real GPU. Screen size, colour depth and device pixel ratio are canned. Fonts differ. Canvas and AudioContext fingerprints come out different.
  • Declared identity: headless Chrome still sends a containing . It also sets to . That property is a W3C standard, "a standard way for co-operating user agents to inform the document that it is controlled by WebDriver". Chromium sets it for , for , and for , the channel Playwright uses to talk to the browser. Note that the last two apply whether the browser is headless or not. The --disable-blink-features=AutomationControlled argument hides the property, but it's no guarantee.
  • Missing JavaScript objects: and the plugin list used to be empty in headless Chrome. Chrome unified headless and headed modes in version 112. Since version 132, the old mode only survives as the standalone binary. That's the binary Playwright's default headless mode runs on, so the old signals still apply there.
  • Irrelevant GUI data: equals in headless, because there's no window frame around the page. In a real window, they differ.
  • Behaviour: no mouse movement, no scroll, instant form fills, and page loads never request favicons or prefetches.

I experienced two components that implemented one or more of the above:

  • Cloudflare Turnstile confirms web visitors are real and blocks unwanted bots without slowing down web experiences for real users. It's a simple snippet of free code that eliminates CAPTCHAs. With Turnstile, you can deliver better experiences and strengthen privacy for all users.

The product doesn't decide the level; the site's configuration does. I met Turnstile on one site where a headed browser passed, and on another where it didn't.

To get past most of them, use a headed browser. You can steer it with Playwright, or any other browser automation API. Unfortunately, it means you need a system with a GUI, or somehow manage to forward the display to an X server. It works perfectly for me on my personal laptop.

Some sites needed two more things:

A persistent browser profile

When a human clears the challenge once in a profile, the browser gets a clearance cookie. Cloudflare documents it:

A cookie proves to Cloudflare that the visitor is a verified human and has passed Cloudflare's client-side verifications. The cookie is securely tied to the specific visitor and device it was issued to, preventing reuse across machines.

Copying the cookie into a fresh browser context doesn't work: the fingerprint of the browser presenting the cookie must match the one that earned it. I tested it on the same site the same day: a fresh context got an unsolvable challenge; the reused profile got no challenge at all.

Not the Chromium that Playwright bundles! Playwright's launch_persistent_contexthandles both:

context = await pw.chromium.launch_persistent_context(
    user_data_dir=".browser-profiles/some-site",             # 1
    channel="chrome",                                        # 2
    headless=False,                                          # 3
    args=["--disable-blink-features=AutomationControlled"],  # 4
)
  1. Persistent profile: cookies, local storage, and the clearance live here
  2. Branded Google Chrome instead of the bundled Chromium

Clear the challenge by hand once, and never close the context at the end of a script: closing it closes the session.

Even headed browsers can't defeat advanced protections. More precisely, headed browsers launched by the automation tool can't. On one site, I used an automated headed browser when in front of the computer. The website showed an "I'm a human" CAPTCHA checkbox. I clicked it. Several times. To no avail.

Here's what I measured on that site, with the same stored profile in both cases:

Playwright, headed, disabled, profile previously cleared by a human

Empty body, no challenge served at all

The shell, with , then Playwright attached to it

Page content, seven cookies including the clearance

Everything is the same, except who launched the browser. The site somehow sniffs the launch method, before even offering a challenge!

I don't know which signal it uses. Playwright launches Chrome with a list of switches of its own: , , , --disable-field-trial-config, a long list, and . One known difference: Chromium sets for , but for only when the port is . On port 9222, the property stays without any extra flag.

The conclusion is pretty straightforward: launch Chrome yourself, and let the automation tool attach to it.

/Applications/Google\ Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google\ Chrome \
  --remote-debugging-port=9222 \
  --user-data-dir="$PWD/.browser-profiles/some-site" \
  --no-first-run --no-default-browser-check &

Solve the challenge once in that window, by hand. Don't navigate while the challenge runs. Then attach:

browser = await pw.chromium.connect_over_cdp("http://127.0.0.1:9222")
context = browser.contexts[0]                                          # 1
page = await context.new_page()                                        # 2
await page.goto(url)
text = await page.evaluate("document.body.innerText")
await page.close()
  1. The existing context, with the cleared profile
  2. A new tab per fetch; close the tab, never the context

Playwright documents, and warns that it "is significantly lower fidelity than the Playwright protocol connection". Some events don't fire. I read the page text and parse it myself instead of intercepting responses.

These switches will no longer be respected if attempting to debug the default Chrome data directory. These switches must now be accompanied by the switch to point to a non-standard directory.

There's no warning on the console and no error in the window. Chrome starts normally, and the port just isn't there. The symptom is curl http://127.0.0.1:9222/json/version failing to connect while shows the flag on the command line.

The second one is just as silent. Launching Chrome while another instance uses the same profile hands the launch over to the running instance. The debugging port never opens. Quit Chrome fully first.

Not every automation-hostile site becomes reachable once a human drives the browser. One site detected my own, hand-driven, everyday Chrome. There was no CAPTCHA to solve and no clearance to earn. I gave up and found the data on a mirror.

Paywalls are the same story. A site that masks fields for free-tier accounts isn't detecting bots; no browser trick reveals them.

Rate limiting is orthogonal to all the levels above. On one site, after half a dozen rapid requests, everything stopped working at once: , Playwright, and my own hand-driven everyday browser got the same refusal. The site had blocked my IP, regardless of the client behind it.

I tried to connect through a VPN, which gave me another client IP, and the site worked again immediately. For later runs, I self-throttled with a between requests and never hit the limit again.

Another site caps the number of search queries per day, regardless of the client. There's no trick there either: treat a capped query as not run rather than as a negative result.

Works, or 403 without a /

Empty page, challenge page, or "enable JavaScript"

Challenge that never resolves headless, content to a window

Headed Chrome, persistent profile, one manual clearance

403 or an unsolvable CAPTCHA to a Playwright-launched window

Shell-launched Chrome with and ,

Your own browser is blocked

Hope you find another source

Everything fails at once, whatever the client, after a burst of requests

items.title: Police Seize Robot that Sexually Assaulted Teen Girl
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Slashdot reader alternative_right shares a story that has drawn international attention for being potentially the first documented instance of a robot being used directly in a sexual assault. According to the Associated Press, German police have opened a sexual harassment investigation after a robot allegedly touched a 16-year-old girl's buttocks and made thrusting motions while two young men reportedly filmed and streamed the incident. Investigators seized the robot and the suspects' phones and are trying to determine whether the movements were preprogrammed or controlled in real time. From the report: Cologne police spokesman Christoph Bermel said the two male teenagers have not been charged but are considered suspects, and investigators were examining whether the robot's movements were preprogrammed or controlled in real time.
 
Police were unfamiliar with this type of incident, he said. "We have not been aware of this phenomenon so far," Bermel told The Associated Press, saying it was "new territory for us." [...] The robot, said to be 120 centimeters (about 3 ft 11 inches) tall, was dressed in a white tank top, black sweatpants and wearing a gold chain and sunglasses. It also had what appears to be a fake mustache. Videos circulated on the internet show two young men escorting the robot toward a group of women, bumping into one and hugging others, on a lively nighttime street.

items.title: Ubuntu 26.10 Released
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
prisoninmate shares a report from 9to5Linux: Ubuntu 26.10 (Stonking Stingray) has been released today, and it is now available for download for those eager to update their Ubuntu systems to a newer release. Powered by the upcoming Linux 7.3 kernel series, Ubuntu 26.10 ships with the latest GNOME 51 desktop environment, TPM-backed full disk encryption (FDE) support on computers without a hardware root of trust, updated Settings to show whether a computer is certified for Ubuntu, and 100% Rust coreutils.
 
There are several App Center enhancements in Ubuntu 26.10, such as a unified app-details view for Snap and Debian packages, a dedicated Drivers page where you can review the available graphics drivers, including NVIDIA driver branches, and support for installing codecs for one-time playback when a media file uses a codec that's not installed.' Other additions include an optional, locally processed AI-powered speech-to-text tool called Myna, system-wide controls for disabling Ubuntu Insights data collection, and better integration with Microsoft Entra ID. Also worth mentioning are the security and software updates that will be available for nine months, through July 2027.

items.title: IMF Warns of the Real AI Threat: Debt
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
"Along with the dangers of continuing cyberattacks, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) reports that the threat of an AI market crash is putting the global markets at risk," writes Slashdot reader databasecowgirl, citing the IMF's latest semiannual Global Financial Stability Report. Here's a summary: Three salient risks could trigger a sharp tightening of financial conditions and market turmoil. Weaker or less durable investment and profitability in artificial intelligence could lead to a correction in AI-related asset prices, amplified by rising leverage and concentrated exposures. Resurgent inflation or fiscal concerns could drive a sharp rise in sovereign bond yields, with potentially broad repercussions across financial markets. Meanwhile, increasingly sophisticated cyber threats pose growing risks as finance becomes more digital and interconnected.
 
Underlying financial vulnerabilities could amplify these risks and turn market stress into systemic events. Although the global banking system remains broadly resilient, pockets of weaker banks persist. Liquidity mismatches among insurers and pension funds have increased, while rising leverage and contingent liquidity risks in private credit could amplify stress.
 
While hedge funds support market functioning in calm times, their use of leverage and exposure to crowded trades could exacerbate market stress too and create spillovers to prime brokers. Some emerging markets have seen policy buffers erode, and frontier economies have increasingly relied on less transparent forms of financing.
 
Finally, although markets for tokenized assets remain small and could offer efficiency gains in several areas, they can create new channels for the buildup of leverage and mismatches in liquidity and maturity, in addition to elevating risks related to technology and infrastructure. These vulnerabilities underscore the need for policies that strengthen resilience, enhance transparency, contain excessive leverage, and improve preparedness for future shocks. The full report can be found here (PDF).

items.title: Flock CEO Defends Surveillance Tech Amid National Backlash
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from TechCrunch: Flock's founder and CEO Garrett Langley doesn't think the risks of introducing surveillance technology at scale outweigh the rewards. "If we want to live in a society where, if you commit a crime, you have a higher probability of being held accountable, we shouldn't pause progress," Langley said, speaking onstage during a panel at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 in San Francisco on Wednesday.
 
During the interview, the controversial founder of the surveillance maker of license plate cameras and other recording devices deflected hard questions about the criticism Flock now faces -- which has since led to canceled contracts and even layoffs. Instead, Langley tended to respond to questions with anecdotes from conversations with police chiefs and city leaders across the United States, and tales of the supposed numerous crimes Flock has solved, rather than offer tangible solutions to people's concerns.
 
In doing so, Langley positioned Flock as an advance in technology that was somewhat inevitable. He stressed that if people wanted to live in a better society -- that is, one with reduced crime -- they would have to offer up their privacy in return. [...] "Technology, at its core, in its definition, is just doing things better. It's not doing things perfect," he said. "Driverless cars, I think, is a fair analogy. Driverless cars, I think, are definitively safer than human drivers. And when there's one accident, I don't think the answer is to shut down driverless cars. The answer is to say, 'Hey, let's talk about how we prevent more accidents in the future.'"
 
[...] From Langley's answers, it's clear that the ethics around how Flock should be used is a decision he would much rather leave up to others. "We don't want to tell city leaders how to do their job," he noted. "We will provide recommendations, we'll provide defaults, but we're going to minimize the number of mandated features, functions, and policies," he said. Langley went on to argue that society too often judges technology "not on how it compares to the past, but how it compares to perfect." He acknowledged that "Flock is far from perfect" but maintained that its technology helps police departments compensate for staffing shortages and improve public safety.
 
When pressed about potential abuse and privacy concerns, Langley offered few specifics, instead arguing that safeguards could be implemented without disrupting police operations. He insisted the benefits of what Flock offers outweigh the controversy. "There's millions and millions of people who have a better life today because [of] Flock," he said, adding that "it's worth it because one day they might be a victim."

items.title: Targeted ads delivered 0-click exploits to install mercenary malware
items.author: Dan Goodin
items.content:
Researchers say that mercenary hackers laced ads with zero-click exploits that installed sophisticated malware on the devices of targeted individuals when they did nothing other than load a website or open an installed app.

The finding, published Thursday by the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab, said the incident is likely to be the first confirmation of zero-click mercenary spyware delivered through targeted ads. The attacks, which worked on iOS and Android devices, are particularly pernicious because they work without requiring any interaction from the target and are invisible unless users run special forensic hardware or software. Citizen Lab said it confirmed that AdFection, as it named the campaign, infected 45 devices at international media organization Al Jazeera in 2024 and 2025.

“This investigation should… serve as a clear warning signal to news organizations around the world that they may be being actively targeted via this new threat,” Citizen Lab researchers wrote. “This targeting may happen both in newsrooms and to individual journalists, editors, and other staff members.” Their report went on to say: “The distribution of spyware via targeted ads represents a security risk not only for potential victims but also for states and civil society at large.”

items.title: First-Ever Public Confirmation of 'Zero-Click' Spyware Delivered Via Targeted Ads
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Citizen Lab says it has documented the first publicly confirmed case of zero-click mercenary spyware being delivered through targeted online ads, a technique it calls "AdFection." "There has been a lot of buzz that online ads can be used to identify and automatically hack targets with pinpoint precision, but now for the first time, we have concrete technical evidence showing this process in action," said Bill Marczak, a researcher at Citizen Lab. The Guardian reports: Citizen Lab, a digital investigations research unit at the University of Toronto, said it believed dozens of devices at the Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera had been compromised by spyware delivered through ads run by Discover-Tech, which describes itself as a specialised digital advertising agency. According to Citizen Lab, Discover-Tech operates a software platform called Controlium that allows its clients to "mass-profile and deanonymize" internet users then covertly hack targets with third-party spyware. Unlike infections that rely on people interacting with links or files, the spyware requires no interaction from the victim to be installed, making it a new delivery technique, Citizen Lab says. The infections happen without a user's knowledge, and in a matter of seconds, according to Citizen Lab.
 
"[The online advertising] ecosystem is being weaponized at a massive scale to profile millions of users, then silently infect targets with zero-click mercenary spyware," the report says. According to the report, Controlium is able to harvest a user's identity and IP address when the user is shown a seemingly benign custom-created ad -- for example, for a digital game or a telecoms service. If the user has been selected as a target for hacking, a mercenary spyware firm can then send a malicious code containing spyware to their device, the researchers say. They say that millions of users worldwide have been served ads by Discover-Tech since 2024, including in Yemen, Brazil, Mexico and Czechia. [...] The full extent of the targeting allegedly enabled by Discover-Tech is unknown. Citizen Lab's findings join mounting evidence that the opaque arrangements underpinning the world of online advertising can be leveraged for surveillance.
