items.title: Nobody Owns "New Media." a16z, Draymond Green, OpenAI, and Even The White House All Claim It
items.author: Tech Media Bias [Research Publication]
items.content:
Andreessen Horowitz, Draymond Green, the White House and OpenAI now share a label. Each calls its own channel "new media." a16z built a New Media team. Green named his production company The New Media. The White House created a "new media seat" in the briefing room. OpenAI bought TBPN, the show that maps who counts as new media.

None of them owns the phrase. Each uses it to describe the same move: the subject of the coverage takes over the microphone. That is a real shift, and it deserves a name. But "new media" is a decades-old academic term, and the people now claiming it are mostly the ones journalists used to cover.

The academic canon is Lev Manovich. In his introduction to , he defined new media through eight propositions. One of them predicted the term's expiration: once most culture is distributed through computers, "new media" stops being new.

That old definition was about format: bits instead of ink. The 2020s definition is about power: who holds the microphone. The phrase is the same, but the meaning has changed.

A Short History of Who Has Claimed "New Media"

The phrase has changed owners roughly every decade. It started with educators, passed to a New York trade group and then to academic journals, was handed to users, and was picked up by political campaigns. Only recently did it reach athletes, venture firms and AI companies.

2022–2026 | The subjects take it. Draymond Green, Andreessen Horowitz, the White House and OpenAI's TBPN deal follow, each covered below.

The pattern runs in one direction. Each new owner sits closer to the subject of coverage and further from the reader. In 2006, Time handed the phrase to the audience. Twenty years later, the people being covered have taken it back.

Every Time Draymond Green Said It

Draymond Green has said "new media" so often that he turned it into a company. The documented record runs from 2022 to now:

The June 2022 Finals episode is the fullest version of his definition. Green set up in the TD Garden press room with Klay Thompson, Andre Iguodala and Gary Payton II. He had been criticized for podcasting between Finals games, and he promised to keep releasing episodes no matter the result. He went after ESPN for giving the Warriors a 20 percent chance to win and Fox Sports' Nick Wright for doubting Steph Curry. Then he laid out the rules: stand on your word, don't chase controversy, give credit when it's due, and teach the game. He named J.J. Redick and C.J. McCollum as fellow members.

Every Time Andreessen Horowitz Said It

Andreessen Horowitz capitalized it, staffed it and put it in the main navigation. In a little over a year, "New Media" went from a team name to a product a16z sells founders during a pitch.

  • a16z's New Media team launched around mid-2025; by June 2026 the firm was marking its first anniversary. It now sits in a16z's site navigation as its own section, a16z.com/new-media, beside the newsletters and podcast network.
  • November 6, 2025, the manifesto. Erik Torenberg, Alex Danco, Henry Williams and Brent Liang published "What is New Media?" It describes a team that helps founders win attention online, an in-house video studio pitched as "the A24 of a16z," packaged launch campaigns and New Media staff who embed inside portfolio companies.
  • January 2026, the fellowship. a16z opened an eight-week New Media Fellowship for operators, creators and storytellers, meant to place trained talent inside portfolio companies.
  • June 18, 2026, the anniversary essay."New Media, One Year In" defined the term as "go-direct as a service" for startups. It listed the owned channels behind it: an X account with a million followers, a newsletter with a quarter million subscribers and a podcast with a million monthly downloads.

The strategy goes back to the firm's founding myth. a16z says Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz modeled the firm on Michael Ovitz's Creative Artists Agency, which helped actors build franchises outside the studio gatekeepers. New Media extends that idea from founders' careers to founders' narratives. The same post describes the team as venture's Formula One pit crew: the general partners drive, and the media team changes the tires. It also commits to shipping the a16z podcast and newsletter five times a week.

The anniversary essay adds the sales mechanics. a16z pitches New Media to founders during what competitors call the Bear Hug, the reverse pitch where the firm sells itself to the startup. It cites launch results from World Labs, whose co-founder Fei-Fei Li credited the team with a launch video shot on a 3D LED stage. It also endorses a friend's definition from an essay titled "New Media is Insider Media", which opens with a line a16z quotes approvingly: "Insider Media is media for insiders, by insiders." a16z's only disagreement with that essay is about whether being in the in-group is positive-sum.

The most revealing lines are a16z's own admissions. The anniversary essay concedes that new media isn't actually new. It says the New Media-branded job postings are mostly classic marketing and comms work, and that the real change is in the packaging and branding.

That is the honest definition. For a16z, new media is a venture firm's PR and marketing function, rebuilt around owned channels and given a name that sounds like journalism. The essay all but says so: founders used to choose between being journalism and being PR, and New Media is pitched as the category in between.

Search for organizations that describe themselves as "new media" and a pattern appears. Very few are newsrooms. Most are government offices, investors, platforms or the subjects of coverage.

TBPN, the daily live tech show hosted by John Coogan and Jordi Hays, publishes the New Media Map that a16z boasted about. In April 2026, OpenAI acquired TBPN and placed it in its Strategy organization. OpenAI's announcement says the show reports to Chris Lehane. OpenAI promised editorial independence, but the arbiter of who counts as new media now belongs to one of the companies it covers.

covered above, complete the list: an NBA forward who trademarked the phrase and a venture firm that staffed it.

Only the White House seat explicitly admits journalists. The rest belong to someone being covered: an athlete, an investor, an AI lab or a newspaper chain that wanted a modern-sounding parent. That is what "new media" means in practice today: the subject owns the channel.

Search the bare phrase "new media" and neither a16z nor Draymond Green shows up near the top. The results are still the textbook version of the term.

Three forces explain this.

A two-word generic phrase reads as a definition request. Search engines answer definition requests with reference sources, not brands.

Wikipedia, IEEE, publishers and universities have linked to the academic meaning for decades. a16z's "What is New Media?" is less than a year old. Even its title is a definitional query, and it still sits behind the encyclopedia.

Branded claims rank for branded queries. a16z's New Media page targets "a16z new media." Green's Audacy deal coverage attaches "The New Media" to his name. The White House wins "new media seat." Each claimant controls a modifier, not the term itself.

This matters beyond SEO. The pages search engines trust are also the pages AI models learn from and cite. Ask an answer engine what new media is, and it will likely give you Manovich, not Marc Andreessen. That is the quiet answer to who owns the phrase: the reference corpus does, and the reference corpus still says it means digital, interactive media.

Nobody owns the phrase. Green's filing covers a branded mark, "The New Media by Draymond Green," not the two words anyone can use. a16z owns a team name and a URL. The White House owns a chair. OpenAI owns the show that draws the map.

There is a second definition worth fighting for. It puts the reader at the center, not the speaker. In this version, new media is wherever people, and now AI models, go to learn something. It is built by contributors who know the subject, and it is distributed on channels the publisher controls. Its test is whether the reader learned something true, not whether the founder won the day online.

Manovich predicted the term would stop being new once culture moved onto computers. It did. The fight now is not over the phrase. It is over whether "new media" describes the people talking or the people learning. For now, the people talking are winning.

items.title: How I Discovered That Most of My Backtesting Decisions Were Coin Flips
items.author: Geoff Cox
items.content:
This is a story about how I found out that most of the decisions in one of my research logs were coin flips, and about what I changed so that it wouldn’t happen again.

In September 2026, I ran the same research model eleven times. The code, the data and the settings were identical each time, and the only thing I changed was the random seed. The best of those eleven runs scored about twice as well as the worst.

That would just be a curiosity if I hadn’t spent months making decisions by comparing a single run against a single other run. When we went back through the research log for that model, 14 of the 21 decisions it recorded, mostly about whether to keep a feature or throw it out, rested on a difference smaller than what the seed alone could produce.

If you’re new to this, here’s a bit of background. I build models that pick stocks, and I can’t test one by waiting ten years to see how it does. So, I backtest it: I replay history, let the model make its picks as if it were living through each date, and score those picks against what actually happened next. I also run hyperparameter searches, which backtest hundreds or thousands of versions of a model with different settings and compare them. Over the last couple of years, that has added up to a lot of models.

In my last post, I wrote about leakage, where information from the future sneaks into the replay and makes a backtest look better than anything you could have done for real. This post is about two other ways of fooling yourself: noise, and the choices you make as the researcher. They’re harder to catch, because neither of them is a bug in the code.

It started with a rerun. Earlier in 2026, I had measured what my live trades actually cost to execute, and the answer was close to nothing. That made me wonder whether a few research lines that I had already closed deserved a second look, since some of them had been judged with a cost assumption that was now clearly too pessimistic. So, an agent reran some of the old experiments.

When I reviewed the agent’s work, the conclusions held up, but several of the supporting numbers were wrong. Fixing those meant actually running a check that had been skipped, and that check reran a configuration from the old log with the identical command. The log had recorded it as a solid result. The rerun came back negative.

The first question was whether the engine was random at all, and it wasn’t. Two runs with the same seed on the same machine produced results that were identical down to the byte. So, whatever had changed between the original run and the rerun, it wasn’t chance, and the data changes since then became their own investigation.

However, it raised a question that I had never asked. If the engine gives the same answer every time for a given seed, how much does the answer move when the seed changes?

How Much Does a Result Move When Nothing Changes?

First, a little background on why a seed matters at all. The models in that research line were gradient-boosted trees, and like a lot of tree models, each tree is trained on a random subset of the features and a random subset of the rows. The seed decides which subsets. If you change it, you get a different set of trees from the same data, which is supposed to be a detail.

On September 8, 2026, Claude and I held one configuration fixed and ran it with eleven different seeds over the full four-year research window. The best seed scored about twice as well as the worst. From that spread, you can work out the smallest difference between two single runs that you can trust, i.e. a difference that you’d only expect to see by chance about one time in twenty.

Then we went back through the log. It recorded 21 decisions that had been made by comparing one run against one other run, and 14 of them rested on a smaller difference than that. Some were features I had thrown out as harmful, and four were features I had kept because they seemed to help. In other words, the evidence on file couldn’t tell any of those 14 variants apart from the run they were compared against, in either direction.

One of those four soon confirmed it. A later rerun, done properly this time with the same seed on both sides, found that a feature the log had recorded as helping was actually hurting. That’s exactly what you’d expect from a difference inside the noise, since it can come out either way.

Fortunately, none of those features were in production, so nothing needed reverting. But the same habit of comparing one run against one other run was also in my more active research lines. When we measured the noise for the daily research engine the same way, one recorded decision stood out. In a long/short research line, which buys some stocks and bets against others by shorting them, the time of day to trade had been chosen on a difference between 17 and 29 times smaller than that engine’s noise. In other words, the backtest couldn’t separate the candidate times at all. The same measurement also showed that the worst loss from peak to trough was even more sensitive to the seed than the score was, and more than doubled between the gentlest seed and the harshest.

So, when does my live system trade? Shortly after the open rather than at the opening bell, and I’d defend that without any backtest. The first stretch after the market opens is the most volatile part of the day, which makes it hard to hit a price target or to model the price you’ll actually get. That reasoning is about how the market works, and no seed can flip it.

The rules that came out of all this are short:

  1. No feature is declared harmful, or kept, on a difference smaller than the measured noise.
  2. Comparisons either use the same seed on both sides, or run several seeds per side and compare the averages.
  3. The seed, the number of threads and where the data came from are stamped into every recorded result, so that any number in the log can be reproduced.

There was one more surprise in the details. The library we were using doesn’t pick a random seed when you don’t give it one. It uses fixed defaults, so every “unseeded” run in the log had been perfectly reproducible all along, and had been sitting on one arbitrary draw that nobody had recorded or varied. Moreover, setting the seed to 0 doesn’t reproduce those runs, because it overrides the defaults with different values. The agent had assumed that it would, and there’s now a test that pins the fact that it doesn’t.

This was tough to learn, as it had taken me a lot of time to engineer myself into those conclusions. Once the coin flips came to light, I kept pushing to see if there was a way to improve the statistical significance of my results. That question, how long it takes before you can tell a real edge from luck, runs through the rest of this post.

Can I Rebuild an Index Fund From Scratch?

A couple of weeks later, I wanted a fair comparison for my own model: something cheap and simple that I could hold it up against, over long stretches of history that included real bear markets. The obvious candidate was a public momentum index fund, which holds the stocks that have risen the most over the past year. It’s one of the cheapest and best-known ways to buy a simple stock-picking rule, which makes it a fair bar for any model that picks stocks. The problem was that the fund only goes back to 2015, and its index’s history before that is the index provider’s own backtest.

So, the plan was to rebuild the index from its published rules, using my own data, and run it back through history myself.

The catch is that a rebuilt index involves a lot of choices, e.g. how far back to measure momentum, how to size each position and when to rebalance (reshuffle the portfolio), and every one of them is a knob. If I build the benchmark, look at how my model compares, and then adjust the benchmark, I’ve tuned my own yardstick.

To avoid that, the spec was written first and merged before any construction code existed. It included a gate that the rebuild had to pass over the years where the real fund exists: its annual return had to land within three percentage points of the fund’s, its risk-adjusted return (how much it earned for how bumpy the ride was) had to be within a fixed margin, and its returns had to move with the fund’s, period by period, with a correlation of at least 0.8, where 1 means moving in lockstep. All three had to pass or the rebuild was disqualified. The spec even explains why it was written first: every parameter is a researcher degree of freedom, and my research log already had four results on record that had been retracted after a closer look.

Writing the gate first wasn’t a new habit for me. When working with LLMs, I’ve found that you have to have very clear acceptance criteria, especially if you want an agent to run unsupervised for long periods of time. I set the initial rules and then refined them with the models.

There was one more guard. The benchmark was deliberately not registered as one of my models, as registered models can be fed into the hyperparameter search. Otherwise, someone, or more likely an agent, could have swept the benchmark’s own parameters and kept the best-scoring version. Changing it requires editing the code, which shows up in the history.

On September 23, 2026, the first build failed the gate by a wide margin. The leading suspect was that it weighted every stock equally, while the real index weights by company size. So, the second build pulled historical share counts from EDGAR, the SEC’s filing database, and weighted by size. That closed about a tenth of the gap, and it failed again.

That second failure was actually useful. A pass would have justified buying a commercial dataset to reach further back in time, but closing only a tenth of the gap meant that better share counts weren’t the problem. So, I found out that the data wasn’t worth buying without having to buy it.

Was That Moving the Goalposts?

This is the part I’ve thought the hardest about how to tell honestly, because the spec said that if the gate failed, the work stopped. It failed twice, and I didn’t stop.

What changed was the diagnosis. The benchmark had been built to rebalance on my model’s dates, roughly once a month, so that a comparison between the two would only differ in how they picked stocks. Meanwhile, the gate asked it to track a fund that rebalances twice a year. Those two requirements contradict each other, so the gate was close to impossible to pass by construction, and both failures had to be read in that light.

So, the work split into two builds with different jobs. The first is a faithful replica on the fund’s own twice-a-year schedule, and its only purpose is to pass the gate and prove that the index can be recreated from my data at all. The second is the monthly build that my model gets compared against, which is then justified by the replica passing. The thresholds never moved, and each new attempt was written up as its own issue, with the reason it might close the gap, before it was run.

On the fund’s own schedule alone, the replica still failed. Then it was weighted by the shares available to public investors (the free float, which is what the index uses), rather than every share a company has issued, and it passed. That happened in the third pull request of the day, about an hour and a quarter after the first failure was merged.

That being said, I don’t think “the thresholds never moved” settles it. A gate that you’re allowed to keep attempting is a search of its own, and with enough attempts, something will eventually pass. What convinced me that this one hadn’t just been searched into passing was the next step.

What If You Fit to Holdings Instead of Returns?

A replica that matches the fund’s return could still be holding the wrong stocks, as lots of different portfolios produce similar returns over a few years, especially when they’re all tilted the same way. However, the fund has to file its actual holdings with the SEC, so there’s a much harder target available: the list of roughly 100 companies it held at each rebalance, and how much of each it held.

So, with the gate already passed, Claude compared the replica against those filings. The first result said that where the replica held the same company as the fund, it sized it almost exactly right, but about a third of the companies were different.

Two bugs in the comparison itself came out along the way. It had been pitting a freshly rebalanced replica against holdings from months after the fund’s last rebalance, and the code that matched company names to tickers had been quietly dropping as much as a third of the fund’s holdings. For example, a check for " CO" ate the “Cos.” in “Marsh & McLennan Cos., Inc.,” which then matched nothing. After both fixes, the replica still disagreed with the fund on about a third of the companies, so the difference was real and it was in how the replica ranked stocks.

Part of that ranking was still a guess, and the agent couldn’t read the index provider’s methodology document, because the provider’s site blocked automated downloads. So, it swept the uncertain parameters and scored each setting by how many of the fund’s actual holdings the replica matched, never by return.

One sweep found that the index measures momentum about 42 trading days before each rebalance, rather than on the rebalance date itself. That moved the share of matching companies from about two thirds to about 80%, and it did better on the filings that were held out of the sweep, which it never saw while choosing, than on the ones it was fitted to.

Another sweep, over how many weeks of volatility (how much a stock’s price swings) to measure, came back flat across a tenfold range. That turned out to be the clue, as the form was wrong rather than the length. A line in the fund’s own documentation described volatility as measured on daily returns, not weekly, and on the holdings, one year of daily returns beat the old assumption on the held-out filings. A shorter window won on the filings it was fitted to and lost on the held-out ones, which is what overfitting looks like: a setting that fits the quirks of the data it was tuned on rather than the real pattern. So, the agent took the round one-year value instead.

Neither change was chosen by the gate, and the commit messages say so when the gate didn’t cooperate. The lag narrowed the return gap, while two of the gate’s other measures got slightly worse. Switching to daily volatility didn’t move the return gap at all, and it was adopted on the strength of the documentation and the held-out holdings.

Then I downloaded the methodology document by hand, and its appendix confirmed both. Volatility is the “standard deviation of daily price returns,” and momentum is measured between month-ends ending two months before the rebalance, which from a late-March rebalance is about 42 trading days. That’s exactly the lag the sweep had found! The document also corrected a couple of things we had guessed wrong, including the cap on how much any one company can weigh and the order of the rules for keeping existing holdings, and those brought the gap down to under one percentage point.

I think this is the most useful thing I took from the whole exercise. Fitting the same parameters to returns would have picked a volatility window that, measured against the holdings, didn’t matter at all, and I would have declared the spec identified. On the other hand, matching about 100 specific companies across 13 real rebalances isn’t something that a single free parameter does by luck. So, if you’re validating a model or a reconstruction, look for the target that is hardest to hit by accident, and fit to that.

The Gate Was Green, but Were the Numbers Right?

The replica still only started in 2011, because the free source of company sizes it used begins around then. To reach back further, Claude and I used the same trick as in my last post. An S&P 500 index fund holds every company in the index in proportion to its size, and it has filed those holdings with the SEC going back to 1995. So, the value of each holding in those filings tells you the company’s size on that date.

The longer replica passed the gate again on the years where the real fund exists, with about 81% of its companies in common with the fund and an average weight error of 0.13 percentage points against the fund’s own filings.

Then I reviewed it, and the review still found three wrong numbers:

  1. The daily return series silently dropped one real day of returns in every rebalance period. After the fix, it agreed with the period-by-period returns, and a regression test now pins that.
  2. For a company that joined the index between two filings, a fallback took its size from the next filing. That’s leakage, since it uses a filing nobody could have seen yet, which is my last post in a single sentence. The effect was small, but the default is now strictly point-in-time, i.e. it only uses what was known on each date.
  3. Prices jumped at the point where one data vendor’s history hands over to another’s, so the long runs were redone on a single source, and the seam is filed as its own bug, which is still open.

The way I do these reviews isn’t sophisticated. On delicate or complex work, I ask a model to go through the result and find what’s wrong, often switching to a different model from the one that did the work, and I repeat this until the review stops finding anything major. All three of these turned up after every check had already passed.

Two more findings from that review were about noise rather than bugs. The first was that leaving out the companies that later failed, the survivorship bias from my last post, flattered the result by a measurable amount. It flattered it the most during the dot-com bust, because the missing companies were the ones that collapsed. The second was that shifting every rebalance date by a single week, earlier or later, moved the result about as much as fixing the survivorship bias had. Nobody chooses the calendar date their backtest happens to rebalance on, yet it moved the answer as much as a real data fix.

So, Could It Tell Itself From Luck?

No. After all of that, with a gate written in advance, passed on returns, checked against holdings and reviewed until the review went quiet, the reconstruction gave me 24 years of a momentum index, most of them from before the fund existed. Over those 24 years, its edge over the plain S&P 500 isn’t statistically established, meaning that it isn’t large enough, compared with the noise, to rule out luck.

The reconstruction did what it was built to do. When the edge you’re measuring is small and markets are noisy, telling skill from luck takes decades, not quarters, and even 24 years can fall short. My own model runs into the same wall: on the evidence so far, it isn’t statistically distinguishable from cheaper alternatives. What I decided to do about that is the subject of my next post.

If I were starting a research project like this again, this is the list I’d hand to myself and to every agent working with me:

  1. Measure the noise before the first comparison. Run one configuration across several seeds and work out the smallest difference you can trust.
  2. Write the gate before the build. Freeze the spec and the pass/fail criteria first, with the reason for each, and make the thing you’re testing hard to tune by accident.
  3. Never widen a threshold. If the gate itself turns out to be wrong, say so in writing, split the job and keep the threshold.
  4. Fit to the hardest target you can find, e.g. holdings rather than returns.
  5. Review the work again after the gate passes, with a different model if you can, until the review stops finding things.
  6. Shift your dates. If moving the calendar by a week moves the answer, the answer is smaller than it looks.
  7. Keep the graveyard. Every closed experiment stays in the repo with the gate it was judged against and its verdict, so that the next person, or the next agent, can see what was already tried and why it failed.

This describes software I run on my own accounts. It is not investment advice and I do not offer investment services.

items.title: Meta and Apple Bring Muse Spark Open AI Model to Mac Studio
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Meta has released Muse Spark Open, an 816-billion-parameter open-weight model optimized to run locally across two 512GB M5 Ultra Mac Studios using Apple's MLX framework. Meta says it's the "most capable U.S. open-weight model to date." MacRumors reports: Muse Spark Open has 816 billion total parameters with 42 billion active parameters and a 1 million-token context window. It is meant for coding and agentic work, and Meta says it excels at extended tasks, multi-step reasoning, and software engineering. The new Muse model was tuned to run on Mac Studio, and Meta says the Mac Studio paired with Muse Spark Open is the "best way to run a powerful model on your own desktop."
 
From Meta: "Apple's unified memory architecture lets the M5 Ultra's integrated GPU use up to 512 GB per Mac Studio, so two machines can hold an entire model. And the chip's 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth is fast enough to read the small slice each token needs. The result is two Mac Studios behave like one supercomputer with a terabyte of unified memory." Apple hasn't released the 512GB Mac Studio as of yet, but it's supposed to be coming later this month. It won't be cheap, because the 256GB Mac Studio is already priced over $10,000.

items.title: Forgepoint Raises $9.8M From Primary and a16z Speedrun to Give Factories an AI Sales Team
items.author: Ishan Pandey
items.content:
America spent money on new factories at an annual rate of $171 billion in August 2026, according to US Census Bureau data, more than double the pace of 2021, yet many of the manufacturers meant to benefit from that boom can still make a part faster than they can send a quote for it. Forgepoint, a New York startup building AI coworkers for the manufacturing back office, has raised a $9.8 million seed round to close that gap. The round was led by Primary Venture Partners and a16z speedrun, with angel investors from OpenAI, Brex, Vercel and SoFi also taking part.

Forgepoint's first product is Frank, an AI Inside Sales Rep that handles the request-for-quote to purchase-order process using each shop's own pricing rules and approval steps. The company reached seven-figure annual recurring revenue within six months of launching Frank, while hundreds of engineers, estimators and sales reps now use it every week. The new money will bring Frank to more manufacturers, deepen its integrations with the systems those companies already run and grow the team.

A Manufacturing Market on the Rise

The reshoring of American industry is visible in the concrete being poured, as construction spending on manufacturing facilities held steady at roughly $75 billion a year between 2015 and 2021, then climbed to a peak of $237 billion in January 2025. In August 2026 it was still running at $171 billion, about 2.2 times its pre-boom level. Manufacturing accounted for 9.7% of US GDP in the second quarter of 2026.

New plants and new supply chains mean more requests for quotes reaching the machine shops, foundries, molders and fabricators that supply them. For those suppliers, winning that work depends less on how fast the shop floor can produce a part and more on how quickly the office can price it, check it and send a quote back to the buyer.

Where Factories Lose Time

Decades of investment have automated the shop floor, while the office around it still runs on email, spreadsheets and ageing enterprise systems. A typical request for quote arrives as an email with several attachments and missing specifications, while turning it into a quote can take ten separate steps. An estimator may have to contact the customer, find similar past jobs, build a cost model, get engineering approval, apply margins, enter the pricing into the ERP, produce the quote, update the CRM and then chase the buyer for an answer.

Only a few of those steps need expert judgment, since the rest are handoffs and data entry, which are what stretch a quote from hours into days or even weeks. Frank is built to take on those administrative steps, leaving engineers, estimators and salespeople to make the technical and commercial calls that decide whether a job is worth winning and at what price.

Those delays matter because buyers have stopped waiting, with nearly half of manufacturers expect a vendor to respond within 24 hours, according to a 2025 Gardner Intelligence study cited by Forgepoint, while the expectation has been rising among part buyers for years. A Paperless Parts survey found that 67% of part buyers expected a quote within 24 hours in 2020, up from 53% a year earlier.

A shop that needs a week to price a job is often no longer in the running by the time its quote arrives. Inside sales is therefore a natural place to start, because the speed at which a manufacturer can answer RFQs directly decides how much new business it wins.

Forgepoint's chief executive, Jack Strauss, spent his career in industrials before founding the company, working at Northrop Grumman, in the Advanced Manufacturing practice at Bain & Company and at aerospace systems integrator Xwing. He kept running into the same disconnect, with manufacturers pouring money into automating production while everything before and after it still moved through inboxes and spreadsheets. Strauss argues that the manufacturers he met had strong demand and capable teams, but their best people were losing hours to administrative work. In a market where speed is a competitive advantage, Frank exists to keep jobs moving and leave skilled operators free for the decisions only they can make.

In early 2025, Strauss and co-founder Alex Pareto, previously head of engineering for the spend management organization at Brex, spent months touring plants across the Midwest, shadowing employees and studying how work actually moved through each business. Pareto, now chief technology officer, says the pair approached those visits as if they had been hired to do the job themselves, because they wanted to understand the problem in depth before trying to solve it. They came away convinced that the frontier AI being built in Silicon Valley could remove many of the bottlenecks they had seen on factory floors in the Midwest.

Frank joins a manufacturer much like a new employee would, getting an email address on the company's domain and learning the shop's operating procedures, pricing rules and approval requirements. When an RFQ arrives, he reads the email and its attachments, flags missing requirements and contacts the buyer for clarification, then prepares a quote using the manufacturer's own cost model, surfaces similar historical jobs and routes the draft to the right reviewer. Once the quote is approved, he produces the final document in the company's template, sends it, manages the follow-up and records the correspondence.

Because quoting looks very different from one shop to the next, Forgepoint configures Frank around how each business already works. At a metal service center he matches material lists and cut lengths against the catalog, applies customer-specific pricing and checks inventory, while at a foundry he reviews part files, gathers missing drawing specifications from the buyer and prepares a first draft for an engineer. The same approach extends across injection molding, automation, fabrication, stamping and machining, while the company says it can go live with full integration in under 30 days.

Capturing Knowledge Before It Retires

In a business where 74% of manufacturers employ fewer than 20 people, the retirement of a single veteran estimator can take decades of pricing logic, customer preferences and exceptions with it. A system that records how those decisions were made gives smaller manufacturers a way to keep that knowledge and keep growing without hiring administrative staff at the same pace.

Across its customers, Forgepoint says monthly quote throughput is up an average of 30% while time to quote has fallen by more than 55%, giving skilled operators more time back in their day. Chas Aday, founder and chief revenue officer of SIP Manufacturing, says his team was building quotes by hand and barely keeping up before Forgepoint, whereas now Frank drafts each quote and he can approve it in about two minutes, leaving him more time for customers and less for data entry.

Zach Fredericks, principal at Primary Venture Partners, argues that a manufacturer's ability to grow depends on how much work its team can quote, plan and manage, adding that Forgepoint is giving those teams more capacity, starting with quoting. He says Primary backed Strauss and Pareto because they understand the details of that work and have a clear ambition to take the same approach across the entire manufacturing back office.

The round fits squarely within Primary's current strategy, since the New York firm raised a $625 million fifth fund in February 2026 to write seed checks averaging $5 million to $10 million, with vertical AI among its focus areas, while a16z speedrun invests up to $1 million in each company in its cohort. Angel investors from OpenAI, Brex, Vercel and SoFi round out a cap table that pairs frontier AI and fintech operators with a founding team rooted in aerospace and industrial manufacturing.

Forgepoint's mission is to put best-in-class technology into the hands of American manufacturers, starting with quoting because that is where a slow response most often costs a shop the job. Over time the company plans to apply the same approach to other back-office departments, helping manufacturers compete and grow without adding administrative headcount at the same rate. With factory construction still running at more than twice its pre-2022 pace and buyers expecting answers within a day, the shops that can quote fastest will be best placed to win the work that reshoring brings, which is where Forgepoint intends to make Frank the reason they can.

items.title: Microsoft Says Windows 11 Is Now 'More Responsive', Runs Better On 8GB of RAM
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Microsoft says recent Windows 11 updates have made the operating system up to 20% more responsive by improving memory management and reducing background resource use. "A big part of that work is making smarter use of memory and system resources," says Navjot Virk, corporate vice president of Windows experiences at Microsoft. "We've improved memory management and efficiency across Windows to help keep more of your PC's resources focused on what you're actively doing." The Verge reports: The improvements to memory management now make a "meaningful difference" on PCs with just 8GB of RAM. "Windows can now keep up to 2GB more of your active data in memory instead of moving it to slower storage," says Virk. "For example, on PCs with 8GB of memory or less, Widgets load only when you open them, making more than 200 MB of memory available for your apps and other work."
 
Microsoft has also made Windows Update less disruptive, cleaned up the Widgets section, and finally allowed the taskbar to be repositioned to the sides or top of a display. Windows Hello sign-in has also been sped up, and Bluetooth pairing is more reliable, "including an AirPods pairing experience that's up to 15 seconds faster."
 
The next big step is a new Windows Search experience that's a lot faster and more capable. [...] It's currently available for Windows Insiders, and Microsoft says it will "roll out more broadly later this year."

items.title: Amazon Launches New Bee 'Personal AI' Devices That Listen to Conversations
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Amazon has unveiled two new Bee "personal AI" devices designed to continuously record, transcribe, and analyze conversations: the $75 wearable Bee Frontier and the $100 phone-mounted Bee Eclipse. Amazon says the devices can generate conversation summaries, surface recurring themes, and recommend actions or purchases, while claiming audio itself is never stored and users can delete transcripts and summaries. CNBC reports: The Bee Frontier is an upgraded version of Amazon's existing wearable that can either be worn on a wrist or clipped to clothing. Similar to earlier generations, the Bee Frontier has up to seven days of battery life, but it's also more expensive, costing $75 compared with its $50 predecessor.
 
Amazon acquired Bee, a San Francisco startup known for its always-listening bracelet, in July 2025 for an undisclosed amount. Bee bracelets are equipped with artificial intelligence and microphones that can record, transcribe and analyze conversations. The dual mics on the Bee Frontier have upgraded noise filtering, "so it can take note of what matters and ignore what doesn't, even in noisy environments like a crowded restaurant or open office," Amazon said in a blog post.
 
Amazon also debuted the $100 Bee Eclipse, which functions like other Bee devices, but instead of being worn, the credit card-sized gadget magnetically snaps on to the back of a smartphone. The Bee Frontier is available Thursday, while the Bee Eclipse "will be available soon," the company said.

items.title: FINQ’s AI-Managed ETFs Return Up to 41.56%, Outperforming the S&P 500’s 10.96%
items.author: Kevin John
items.content:
Artificial intelligence is increasingly being used to analyze markets, generate investment signals, and support portfolio decisions. FINQ is pursuing a more ambitious application: placing AI at the center of the investment process itself, with algorithms responsible for ranking stocks, selecting holdings, and determining portfolio weights.

The asset management company reported that its two AI-managed exchange-traded funds had significantly outperformed the S&P 500 since their February 5, 2026 inception. As of September 30, 2026, FINQ’s dollar-neutral ETF, AINT, had returned 41.56%, while its long-only fund, AIUP, had returned 32.66%. The S&P 500 returned 10.96% over the same period, according to the company’s reported figures.

The results place FINQ among the companies seeking to demonstrate that artificial intelligence can do more than assist traditional investment managers. Its approach is built around autonomous portfolio management, with the system continuously evaluating market information and adjusting investments according to its rankings.

Two Strategies, One AI Framework

FINQ’s funds approach the market differently, despite relying on the same underlying investment philosophy.

The FINQ FIRST U.S. Large Cap AI-Managed U.S. Equity ETF (AIUP) follows a long-only strategy, investing in U.S. large-cap equities selected and weighted by the company’s AI framework. The goal is to maintain exposure to highly ranked companies while adapting the portfolio as market conditions change.

FINQ reports that AIUP outperformed the S&P 500 at every month-end since its inception. Its reported return of 32.66% exceeded the benchmark’s 10.96% by 21.70 percentage points.

AINT, the FINQ Dollar Neutral U.S. Large Cap AI-Managed U.S. Equity ETF, takes a different approach. The fund buys stocks that rank highly in its model while selling short those ranked lowest. This structure is designed to capture differences in the relative performance of companies rather than relying exclusively on the broader market rising.

As of September 30, 2026, AINT had returned 41.56% since inception, outperforming the S&P 500 by 30.60 percentage points, according to FINQ's figures. FINQ said the fund had outperformed the benchmark at every month-end except its first month of trading.

The distinction matters because the funds are not simply interchangeable products carrying different names. AIUP provides long-only equity exposure, while AINT uses long and short positions to implement a relative-ranking strategy.

What Makes FINQ’s Approach Different?

Traditional active managers rely on combinations of financial analysis, economic forecasts, company research, and professional judgment. Quantitative funds also use algorithms, but FINQ positions its system as an autonomous framework that evaluates index constituents and makes portfolio decisions without discretionary human stock selection.

According to the company, its proprietary technology systematically analyzes financial and market data for index participants in real time. The system ranks companies, selects securities, and adjusts portfolio weights as conditions evolve.

That process is intended to help the funds respond to changing information at a scale and speed that would be difficult to replicate through conventional manual analysis. However, the distinction between automation and investment performance remains important: a system can process information quickly without necessarily interpreting every market development correctly.

“These results demonstrate the strength and consistency of our AI framework during dynamic market environments,” said Eldad Tamir, founder and CEO of FINQ. “I believe autonomous investing will continue to reshape asset management, and the performance of AIUP and AINT reflects the growing ability of AI to adapt, identify opportunities, and respond to market changes at scale.”

Early Results Are Not a Long-Term Verdict

The performance figures provide an encouraging early data point for FINQ, but the measurement period is still relatively short. Both funds began trading in February 2026, meaning their reported records cover less than eight months.

That limitation is especially relevant when evaluating an investment strategy that claims to adapt to different market environments. A model may perform well under certain conditions and struggle when leadership shifts, volatility increases, or correlations between stocks change.

AINT also introduces short-selling exposure, which can create risks that differ from those of a long-only equity fund. Neither strategy’s reported returns establish that the same performance will persist through a full market cycle.

FINQ’s next challenge is therefore to demonstrate that its approach can sustain its results over a longer period, including less favorable market conditions.

For investors, the September 30 figures offer a snapshot of how the company’s autonomous investing model has performed since launch. They do not guarantee future returns. Investment values fluctuate, and investors may receive less than their original investment when they sell their shares. Current performance may also differ from the figures reported here.

If FINQ can continue to produce competitive results while demonstrating resilience across market cycles, its ETFs could strengthen the case for AI as a portfolio manager rather than merely an analytical tool. For now, the early numbers make the company’s experiment worth watching.
